speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, November 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gardiner (p. 4875).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise and speak on this motion brought forward by my colleague from Prince George- Bulkley Valley. I would like to compliment him on bringing it forth at this point in time in Canadian history. It is important that he has seen the wisdom of reminding Canadians that we have much to be proud of. We must at this point in our discussion of the Constitution and our constitutional problems take time out to be proud that we are Canadians and that we have a heritage that is rich and quite frankly worth bragging about.
Next year will be Canada's 125th anniversary. I think it is very appropriate that this motion is before the House so that it can be passed and that the first Canadian heritage day can be celebrated during our 125th anniversary.
One of the things I think makes Canada unique is the fact that most Canadians have roots in many parts of Canada. Although there are times when we have regional differences and different points of view, most Canadians' when they look back at their family backgrounds have roots in all regions in Canada.
In my own family my grandfather, grandmother and my mother were born in Quebec. They came from the southern townships of Quebec. I have roots in Alberta
where my father settled in Edmonton. I now have roots in British Columbia where I have lived for 40 years.
Because Canadians have roots in all parts of Canada we should have a national heritage day. It should not be a day that celebrates simply British Columbia or Quebec or Nova Scotia, but a day which emphasizes that we are all Canadians and that we have a heritage that is important to remember.
There is no area in Canada that does not have a rich heritage. My own municipality of Surrey, which was named after Surrey, England, is tremendously rich in the heritage of that area. People forget that it was one of the original logging areas. When we look at some of the pioneer pictures we find that particularly the north part of it was covered with massive Douglas fir. They are huge trees. The old pictures show the logging. It was nothing to have a six-foot diameter stump. The oxen and early steam engines dragged the timber out of the bush.
Fortunately for us in Surrey we have one of the best medium sized museums anywhere in western Canada if not in all of Canada. It is called the Surrey Museum. It has been able to capture and preserve a great deal of the history and heritage of Surrey. This is the heritage of the farm community which settled on the Delta between the Serpentine and the Nicomekl Rivers in South Surrey. It comes right up into the north part of Surrey, into what is now part of my riding in Port Kells. These were the original farming areas in the lower Fraser Valley. This is very good rich farming land. There are whole historical areas like the Tynhead area which has now been turned into a provincial park. This is where pioneers settled early on.
We have the Fraser River with its tremendous heritage. The Fraser River as everyone knows was the initial navigation river into the interior. It was the highway on which people went further into the interior in the exploration of British Columbia. It was a busy waterway in its earlier days and it still is for logging. Massive log booms were moved up and down that river. The lumber industry of British Columbia which has become known world-wide and is so much a part of our make-up

actually started predominantly in and around the Fraser River.
We have historical trails like the Semiamo Trail that link New Westminster right down into the United States. It was really our first north-south link with our neighbours to the south.
These are the things that even a small community like Surrey has that is part of its heritage. Surrey has a rich multicultural heritage going back many years with Indo-Canadian families, with Japanese settling in the area and more recently with large ethnic communities such as Portuguese, Italians and Vietnamese. This again enhanced the heritage of our community.
It would be appropriate and fitting as we move toward our 125th anniversary if Canada adopted a national heritage day. That could act as a focal point of unity right across this country. It could say to all Canadians that we are proud. We have a tremendous potential in this country. We have a rich history and diversity, but we have some common goals and we have some common things to celebrate.
Therefore I would urge members on all sides of this House to support whole-heartedly this motion put forward by the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley so that we can pass it and that it can become law within the federal jurisdiction. Then next year, as we celebrate our 125th anniversary of Canada, we could have the first national heritage day.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for recognizing me.
It is a privilege to take part in the debate on second reading of Bill C-236, an act respecting national heritage day, especially since the potential impact of this legislation is quite considerable.
As citizens of this country, we have a right to be proud of our historical and cultural heritage and of the vital contribution made by the men and women who over the years have helped make Canada what it is today, one of the most enviable countries in the world.
We also have a right to be proud of our ancestry, our language and our family and religious traditions, which are so richly diverse. Together, these values reflect not only our attachment to the past but also our admiration for those who shaped that past.
Considering the profound changes taking place in today's society, especially at a time when we are trying to redefine our common future, it is imperative that governments-and each and every one of us-make a more conscious investment in preserving our history and our cultural identity.
Canada, as we all know, represents a unique mixture of traditions and symbols based on our history, our diverse heritage and our historic experience. These traditions and symbols strengthen our sense of community and maintain a continuity between our past and our future.
We have reached a turning point in our history, both nationally and internationally. The constitutional choices we are about to make will not only affect our identity as a nation but also our position in the world.
As a nation we are a confederation, and we want to remain so. This does not mean that the framework for our confederation must remain identical to what it has been so far. We must be creative and show initiative. We must start these discussions with the conviction that we are going to win, that we will create a Canada where everyone will be able to benefit from what this country has to offer.
But how do we do that? Obviously we need a good dose of tolerance and openmindedness, and both tend to increase with our knowledge of the past. Learning about our past does not mean memorizing historic facts and dates but understanding the men and women who made that past. That knowledge will put us in a better position to build our future.
Internationally we want to remain what we are: a prosperous and competitive nation. To do so, we must keep up with the rapid changes taking place in the world. Canada's future prosperity will depend on our ability to take advantage of opportunities and successfully meet the challenges of rapid change in areas such as informatics, biotechnology and telecommunications.
December 9, 1991

It may seem unusual that I should mention those three areas, considering the subject before the House today. In other words, what connection is there between technological expansion and our heritage? A very close one, because unless we have a profound sense of our heritage and the community to which we belong, unless we understand and assimilate our past, we cannot move ahead.
If we look at other countries, those that have learned from their past experience and past mistakes happen to be the same countries that are looking ahead to the future. If we want to build Canada, and if we want to build Canada's future together, we must know our roots. If Canadians are to contribute to the development and unity of this country, they must know what constitutes its foundation.
As I see it, the question is not whether Canadians should celebrate the riches of their heritage but how. Creating a national heritage day could become part of the government's efforts to emphasize the importance of preserving Canadian unity.
It is also true that adding a holiday that celebrates Canada, its people and its accomplishments would complement Canada Day, celebrated every year on July 1. We are one of those countries that tend to understate their heritage. Nevertheless, we have every reason to be proud of our background. Making Canadians more aware of our rich history and of heritage values in general would undoubtedly help to enhance our sense of community as Canadians. Canada Day expresses our pride as citizens of the confederation to which we belong, and National Heritage Day would emphasize our diverse roots and help us gain a better understanding of what was accomplished by the men and women who built the society in which we live today.
It was suggested that we should celebrate National Heritage Day on the third Monday in February, during the longest period in the year without a holiday. We have no objection. It is an excellent idea. I am sure that Canadians would be delighted to have a day's respite in the middle of winter. It would be a good opportunity to spend a few moments to reflect on what our ancestors accomplished. A chance to get back to our roots. It would also be an excellent antidote for the winter blues a real morale booster for workers and for all Canadians.

Furthermore, Canada Day is celebrated during the summer holidays but National Heritage Day would be celebrated during the school year. Our young people would have an opportunity to reflect on their country's past. With their innate curiosity and questing minds, they would make us explore areas that are too often neglected.
Parents, seniors and various cultural groups could be involved in a series of activities organized in our schools to prepare for this day.
If we want future generations to be proud of their identity, proud of belonging to this country, let us give them a chance to learn about the past, to gain a better understanding of the changes that occurred over the centuries and shaped the country we live in today.
However, there are other considerations, and I am referring to this country's economic interests. A holiday would be very costly. In fact, Canada would lose about $2.5 billion as a result. I realize that pride and patriotism cannot be expressed in dollars and cents, but we must be realistic.
We believe that increasing our productivity is the key to increasing the real incomes of Canadians. Considering the present state of our economy, and at a time when we are trying to make our economy more competitive, these figures should make us stop and think. Although we agree with the principle of National Heritage Day, our concern must also be for the economic prosperity of our country.
Creating National Heritage Day might also have a very substantial social impact, since this day would concern only a minority of Canadians. About 8 per cent of the Canadian population would be part of this magnificent day. Finally-I am running out of time; I noticed your signal, Mr. Speaker-to achieve a consensus in this respect we must try and develop in this country a real sense of heritage values and work together to create the kind of economic, social and political climate that such a message requires.
A national heritage day requires broader consultation, and consequently I believe that until we have found a way to let all Canadians share this pride in our heritage, it would be best to proceed as requested.

December 9, 1991
Private Members' Business
[English\

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate my colleague from Prince George-Bulkley Valley for presenting this piece of legislation today. I was sorry to hear from the member who spoke on behalf of the Conservative Party that he is now calling for some delay in considering such a piece of legislation.
Canada's heritage is something we cannot celebrate enough. We should be paying more attention and creating holidays such as this where we can draw Canadians to the values in this country that they should be respecting and celebrating.
At this point the fundamental basis of this country is under attack from many quarters. Many people are concerned that institutions which initially brought this country together such as Canada Post, the national railway system, VIA Rail are now being dismantled. As a result the very sinews that hold the country together are weakening and people are concerned all across this country.
The same is true of the debate around our Constitution and the separation of the province of Quebec. Many Canadians are concerned about what is going to happen to our country in the future. They want to have their concerns focused on the value of keeping this country together and on the heritage of this country that we all treasure.
People are concerned that the promises made many years ago about economic integration of the United States with Canada and other countries in the hemisphere is now being realized. As a result we are losing our national identity. At this time Canadians need something to focus on in order to recognize and pay tribute to the heritage that brought this country together in the first place.
For example, Canada is described as a country that was put together against all odds, even geography. In this hemisphere we have a north-south alignment of the geographical features, the mountains ranges and the Mississippi River valley, et cetera. All these things tend to draw our attention north and south. Yet the Canadians of many years ago built a nation across this country from sea to sea that was able to defeat the dictates of geography. It is that kind of nation we are attempting to keep together 125 years after its founding in 1867. I am
hopeful that we are going to it. We must constantly focus Canadians on the value of their countiy and heritage. At a time when there are tensions in this country that threaten to pull it apart I am concerned that people will be looking outward and will lose concern for their countiy.
A tremendous number of people over many years made great sacrifices to build this countiy and keep it together. I think those sacrifices ought to be honoured and recognized by Canadians. A holiday such as the one proposed by my colleague, a national heritage day, is exactly what we need. Dominion Day or Canada Day is recognized on July 1, but we are one of the countries in the world with the fewest days recognizing our natural heritage. I think the more we have the better off we are going to be. We need to focus people on the value of that heritage.
Many communities across the country are already attempting to do that. For example, I live in a community that grew up around the logging and forest industry. It was a pioneering community in terms of the development of pulp and paper on the west coast of Canada and the development of markets in Asia. The community where I live was a pioneering community in terms of those things. It was a community which really did not pay attention to its heritage until it saw that there was a threat to that industiy and heritage. Members in the community have now revived an old logging road system based on a logging Shay engine, what they called the two-spot. They have revived an old railway station that was about to be tom down. It has been rebuilt on the waterfront and focuses the community on an industry which was very important in building that community.
There is an old pioneer mill, McLean's Mill, in the valley that they are now putting together and rebuilding. They hope to have an old operating sawmill in that community to show people exactly how the forest industry was structured many years ago. It will show what kinds of tribulations workers used to go through to keep the machines operating and the raw materials supplied to that mill.
Many communities across this countiy are looking back into their history and taking things of value from it. They are reviving and emphasizing them and using them to teach children their heritage and show them what kind of values this countiy and its communities had in the past.

Too often over the past 20 or 30 years we have ignored our past. As a result many of the children and young people in our country have lost those values. I think this proposal for a national holiday to celebrate our heritage is a perfect idea to focus our young people on the values that we as Canadians hold and the value of our history.
It would be unfortunate if we took the view that another holiday is simply an additional cost added to doing business. The previous speaker mentioned that a statutory holiday in Canada would cost something like $2.5 billion, but that is only one side of the ledger. We all know that holidays also have an economic value to the country. Canada has fewer holidays for its work force than almost any other country on the globe. I was looking at an article recently in an American magazine where they listed all the holidays people are entitled to in various countries.
In Austria, for example, workers are allowed a minimum of 30 days of holidays per year; Denmark, 30; Sweden, 30; Italy, 28; France, 25; Netherlands, 24; Spain, 22; United Kingdom, 22; Australia, 20; Belgium, 20; Finland, 20; Switzerland, 20; West Germany, 18; and down at the very bottom with 10 minimum holidays a year is Canada.
Many of those countries at the top of the list are countries that are very successful competitors when it comes to competition with Canada. Holidays are not a cost of doing business. They provide value to business. People get time off from work and are able to relax and reduce the kind of stress that builds up in the work place. People get time off work and they acknowledge important holidays.
In addition, when people get time off from work, other people who are currently not employed are able to take their place and as a result we are able to reduce the unemployment level in this country. By reducing unemployment, as many of these countries with more holidays than Canada have done, we may be able to bring people back so they can feel they are playing a larger role in the country, contributing more, and that they are not a net drag on the country's resources and will be much better Canadians as a result.
Private Members' Business
I would ask all members to support this bill to create a heritage day in the third week in February. Again I congratulate the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley who made this proposal.

Mr. Speaker,
I want to say how delighted I am to be able to participate in this debate. I support this bill and I congratulate the member for this motion.
Establishing a heritage day in Canada is not a new idea but it is a very worth-while idea. As a Canadian who loves this country I have always found it a mystery and a conundrum why we have so much difficulty with our identity, why we lack the unity of what is really a very successful country. This is one of the best countries in the world. Millions if not billions of people who inhabit this planet would give their eye teeth to be Canadians, to be citizens of this country.
Here we are, one of the most privileged people in the world living in one of the greatest countries in the world and we have unity problems. We seem to stress the negative. We seem to focus on the things that tend to disunite us as opposed to those things we hold in common, the things that unite us.
The fact of the matter is that unlike our friends south of the border, the Americans, we do not celebrate enough. We do not flaunt our successes enough. We do not show our pride enough. The Americans perhaps go too far because they show their pride and wear their pride on their lapels or on their sleeves. We tend to be shy and diffident. While I would not suggest that we should be just like the Americans, I think we do have to tell the Canadian story because it is a wonderful stoiy.
Unlike America, this country was not bom in revolution. We have a peaceful history. We have had peaceful evolution. We should have great pride in that. We should be very proud. We tend, however, to sit back and be quite defensive about this country. We do not have to be defensive at all. Let us go on the offensive and tell the world how great we are.
I can think of so many things to celebrate. We are coming up to our 125th birthday of Confederation and what a good time it would be to establish a national heritage day. Think of the private sector-public sector partnership we have had in this country. We have had a tremendous partnership. It is one of the reasons for the success of this country. We have not done it just on private moneys or private initiative. We have had a

Private Members' Business
wonderful and very productive partnership involving government and the private sector.
We could think of the CPR, going back to the late 19th century when we established a railroad to the west coast. We could think of the seaway we built with the help of the Americans back in the 1950s. I can think of some of the great public initiatives like the CBC established in the 1930s.
Medicare, established in the 1960s, is still one of the great public health models and is envied, I would think, in most parts of the world. It has some financial problems today but it is a tremendous model, a successful model, a model to be emulated all around the world. We have a lot of things to celebrate.
We should think of our diversity. We should think of the fact that we have been the homeland of peoples from all around the world. People have come from the four corners of the earth to be here, to live here, to establish their families here, to pursue their careers and to contribute to this country.
That is another reason why we are successful. I think we have been able to have the cream of the crop of people from all around the world. We have had the very best come here and establish their lives. We have been the beneficiaries of this immigration.
When I think of a heritage day, I think not only of our diversity but of our multiculturalism which has given us some problem. I think it gives us problems because I do not think we understand multiculturalism very well. We compare it to what is called the melting pot in the United States.
The melting pot of the United States is largely a myth. For example, have the blacks been melted? Have the Hispanics been melted? They have not. There is a tremendous amount of diversity in the United States. There is a tremendous amount of multiculturalism in the United States. The myth persists about the great American melting pot. There is a melting pot at the level of the national anthem, at the level of the Stars and Stripes. It is there with respect to the flag and to good old fashioned American pie. When we get beneath that the United States is just as diverse and just as multicultural as we are.
I think that on heritage day we could explain multiculturalism. It would give us that opportunity. It would give
new Canadians and groups of Canadians bom elsewhere the opportunity to show how great they are as Canadians.
I believe to the very bottom of my heart that it does not matter whether your skin is brown, whether your religion is Islamic, Catholic, or what mother tongue you have: French, English, German, or Swahili. None of those differences stands in the way of being a good Canadians.
When someone asks me what a Canadian is, other than the fact that we all share a common citizenship it is very difficult for me to explain it. I do not identify Canadian according to race, according to colour, according to skin or according to religion. A Canadian is one who lives here, believes in this country, loves this country, has pride in Canadian citizenship and is proud of being a resident of this country.
A heritage day something we need. I think it would give us the opportunity to tell the wonderful Canadian story.
It could explain where we have been, where we are at right now-and we have some difficult times right now-and where we might be going. We have Canada Day on July 1, but we could do with a lot more. It is not unusual for other countries to have a number of days, several days in honour of national heritage.
A member earlier was mentioning Austria with perhaps as many as 30 days set aside to celebrate one way or the another its heritage. In the United States, just next door, there are apparently five national heritage days. Finland has 12.
It would seem to me that this great countiy could afford at least to have one more day. What better time than the cold month of February? This is a cold country and it would be good right in the middle of the winter, after Christmas and New Year's Day, to set aside a day to celebrate this country. We have a lot to celebrate.
I am happy to support this private member's motion. I congratulate once again the mover. I would hope we have a successful vote so that this motion could be examined further in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to speak in favour of this motion instituting a national heritage day and I

would like to congratulate the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley for putting forth this motion.
I would like to start my remarks in context of a quote from a government publication called Proud To Be a Canadian: A Rich Cultural Tradition. This government publication at page 21 stated:
A Heritage Day celebrated nationally would enhance two vital aspects of Canadian identity. We would focus on those parts of our heritage which are truly the expression of what we have achieved together, from our liveable cities to our artistic genius. And we would reach out across our many cultures to learn about and savour the differences our heritage stands for. A Heritage Day, in other words, would be a uniquely Canadian occasion to celebrate both unity and diversity.
I think that paragraph captures what the idea of a national heritage day is all about. It brings together all of those things which make us Canadians and make Canada the country that we believe in.
We have been made up over the past 125 years and before of groups of people from all over the world. We are a mosaic of people who bring to Canada our rich backgrounds, our rich heritage from other places. We bring different languages, different cultures, different ways of looking at things. Over the years we have moulded together in a country I believe we can all be very proud of.
We have our difficulties and we have our problems. We are in the middle of a national unity debate as to whether we should remain as a whole from sea to sea to sea. I do not think there is any doubt in the minds of most of us that the heritage we have has a richness unsurpassed in very short time by any other country.
I remember when I was in high school looking at what they taught us then and thinking at that time in my early teens that Canada was not or did not have a very rich background, a very rich history.
Yet as time went on, through high school I began more and more to realize and to understand how rich our history was and how enriched Canada was. The richness of Canada is something I learned about over many years of reading political history books, political biographies, excellent Canadian publications such as Canadian Forum, Options, Maclean's magazine, to name three, that set out what we, as Canadians see; why we as Canadians stand out in the world.
I wonder throughout this unity debate why it is not important to have a national heritage day to reflect on

how lucky we really are, and how we are viewed, not only internally in Canada, but how we are viewed by other nations around the world.
In talking to people from various other countries, they have a hard time believing that we as Canadians would even consider splitting this wonderful country apart. We have so much going for us, not only nationally but internationally. Looking at our heritage, I am a firm believer that we must take that step further. We must look not only at where we have come from and what we are today, but use this to show us where we should go in the future.
If I could be parochial for a minute, I will look back at Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt and some of the things within that riding and within the area of the Kootenays where I was bom and raised, that I think are so important to our history and so important to our upcoming generations. It is imperative that we protect that heritage and remember the richness of our history, our culture, our art-both visual and performing arts- that make us what we are.
If we look at Christina Lake, there is a group right now trying to preserve and save the Christina Lake or Cascade Powerhouse. It is an important building and an important point in the history of that region. Grand Forks, whose history goes back almost as far as any other community within British Columbia, has a rich heritage in mining. They are at present in the process of trying to preserve the railway station in that area, along with the abandoned rail tracks, to ensure that our heritage is protected.
Up in Penticton we have the ongoing restoration of the S.S. Sicammous, one of the few stem-wheelers remaining. The other stem-wheeler in our region in the riding of Kootenay West, in Kaslo, originally the home of both my father and my wife, is also preserving the S.S. Moyie and have a museum within that structure.
These are important parts of our past. It is important that we look at those parts of our past to ensure that our children understand what we went through and what our parents went through, little bits of the past that help us chart the course for the future.
I also would like to briefly mention how important to our culture and our heritage is art. On the west coast, for instance, there is the art of Emily Carr, an important part of the past, linking the heritage of Emily's back-

ground with the heritage of the community that was built up around her.
All across Canada in the visual arts we have the opportunity and have seen people take the opportunity to ensure that we understand and realize not only what is occurring at that time, what has occurred before and, what I am sure will come and be happening in the future.
Our performing arts such as the National Ballet in Ottawa, the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, the symphony orchestras having such a hard time across Canada whether they be in Vancouver or in any other city, these are important parts of heritage. Focusing on a day where we as Canadians can recall I think is important.
A minor part of that is the need for a day off for all working people of Canada to reflect. It would not simply be to have a day off to enjoy themselves, but for a focus as we have on Canada Day, July 1. It is a focus of the richness of our past, the richness of what we have in the present and the hope that I have of the richness that we will carry on into the future.
It is important. I believe that this House should go to the next stage on National Heritage Day, iron out the bugs that are within this bill and bring it back for third reading, passage and institution. Yes, Canadians want and need a day to recall the past, to remember the present and to ensure that it is reflected in what we do in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I see that there is really only a minute or so left so I will just begin my remarks. If the matter comes back for debate, I would like to complete them at that stage.
I support this bill to establish a national heritage day. It is a very important bill, and I would like to congratulate the member for introducing it. I am disappointed that at least some government members have not said they are going to support the bill. In fact, the parliamentary secretary indicated in what is frankly a rather spurious reason that because the bill only applies to employees within the federal jurisdiction, it does not apply to enough people in Canada for the government to support it.
It seems to me that the government should recognize this bill as a first step. It does deal with those with whom
it is the jurisdiction of Parliament to deal. We can only deal with employees within the federal jurisdiction, and therefore, we ought to exercise that jurisdiction to its full if the idea is a good one. I know that many government members believe it to be fundamentally a good one.
With that, I notice that it is 12 p.m. Perhaps I can continue on the next occasion.

That Bill C-32 be amended by deleting Clause 1.
December 9, 1991



He said: Mr. Speaker, let us make it very clear what is involved here for people who are concerned about this debate.
The government is attempting to extend its discriminatory freeze on Canada Assistance Plan payments to other provinces of which three have been singled out: British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
The Canada Assistance Plan payments to those provinces will not be permitted to increase by more than 5 per cent per year. If this piece of legislation passes, this will hold until 1995. It is a very simple bill and has, in fact, simply one clause in it. To demonstrate our complete opposition to this piece of legislation, to demonstrate how completely unfair we feel this legislation is to the three provinces which are affected, and to the hundreds of thousands of unemployed people across the country who have had to go on to welfare because of the recession which this government created, we intend to move that that entire clause be stricken from the legislation, which of course would leave the legislation null and void.
We think that is in fact the best response to this irresponsible, uncaring and totally unacceptable piece of attempted legislation on the part of a government which does not seem to realize how badly it has hurt men and women and children across this country with the approach it has taken to try to save money, an approach which I have to say in my relatively short period here, about seven and a half years now, is the most heartless approach that I have seen this government or any government take. A more heartless approach I have not seen. It first created a recession. Remember, this has been called the "made in Canada" recession. It has not been called that by those of us in the opposition, it has been called that by the government's friends. The Conference Board of Canada, which is supported by the large-scale business community in this country, said this is a made in Canada recession, brought into effect by this government and this government's failures in economic policy.
Then, having created the recession, this government decided that they would put the following into effect. They would put into effect changes in unemployment insurance which would make it more difficult for workers in those parts of Canada that are being hardest hit by this

recession-British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario-to receive the unemployment insurance to which they were due given their years of contribution.
Let me refer to what those workers found instead of receiving a fair amount of unemployment insurance in the midst of what, in Ontario at least, has been the worst recession since the depression of the 1930s. The figures demonstrate it clearly, I say to the minister on the other side. Like so many ministers on the other side he takes the position that there is nothing but optimism to be seen, nothing but sunshine to see, despite the fact that even Statistics Canada is unwilling to announce this recession is over because it is so clear that this recession is not over and that it is damaging people from coast to coast.
They passed these unemployment insurance changes which forced people who were out of work to turn to welfare and then, to add insult to this further injury, they put into effect this 5 per cent limit on federal government assistance to welfare payments: the so-called cap on CAP, the cap on Canada Assistance Plan aid to the provinces. The consequence to the provinces has been that they have been faced with either letting people starve on welfare or paying themselves for the welfare costs of their people.
Because we are Canadians and because we believe in this country, we do not let people starve. We do not let people face the complete destruction of their lives because of the mismanagement of the federal government. Most provinces have said: "We do not like it. We think it is so unfair that we are going to try to take the federal government to court, but we will still pay these extra costs".
In the case of British Columbia the extra cost of this piece of legislation up to 1995 will be $900 million. In the case of Ontario the estimates for the first two years of this program are $1.7 billion. It is going to cost $1.7 billion in the first two years of this freeze. Alberta has the same kinds of devastating figures. Then the government turns around and blames the provinces for running deficits when what has happened is that this government has systematically forced the provinces either to let their people go hungry, to let them live homeless on the streets or to have a larger deficit which they do not like, a deficit which they would prefer not to run but a deficit

December 9, 1991
Government Orders
which is intended to safeguard the people of then-provinces.
It seems to me that the heartlessness of this government combined with just tragic changes in unemployment insurance so far as people are concerned has led both to a financial crisis for our provinces and to devastating results for people across this country who have had to go on welfare, who have had to see their sense of dignity destroyed in many cases. These are people who have worked-I have talked to them-for 27 or 28 years for a single company and were thrown out of work by the free trade deal that the government has brought into effect. In front of us today the government wants to add insult to injury to further injury by passing this piece of legislation.
I urge this House to accept this amendment, to return this country to sanity and to make the federal government do the job that it is elected to do to safeguard the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that during the private members' hour between eleven and twelve o'clock this morning we were debating a bill about implementing a national heritage day.
I think one of our strong heritages in this country is a program such as CAP, the Canada Assistance Plan. I think it might be wise just to remind viewers what the Canada Assistance Plan is and why it was implemented.
As the mover of the amendment has already said, the CAP was enacted in 1966 to encourage the development and extension of assistance and welfare services programs throughout Canada. Under the plan the federal government has entered into agreements with the provinces and territories to share the costs incurred by provinces, territories and municipalities. This is crucial because the federal government seems to pass on: "That is a municipal affair, that is a provincial affair".
The plan specifically states: "and municipalities in providing social assistance and welfare services to needy Canadians. The primary objectives of CAP are: (1) to support the provision by provinces of adequate assistance and institutional care for persons in need". I underline "support", not cut as Bill C-32 wants to do. It continues:
"(2) to support the provision by provinces of welfare services designed to lessen, remove or prevent the causes and effects of poverty, child neglect or dependence on public assistance". Again, I underline "to support", not to cut as Bill C-32 attempts to do.
Under CAP the federal government contributes 50 per cent of the costs incurred by the provinces and municipalities in providing assistance to persons who are in need regardless of the cause of their need. I want to underline that: "regardless of the cause of their need". The plan goes on to say that it enables the federal government to contribute 50 per cent of certain provincial and municipal costs of providing welfare services to persons who are in need or who are likely to become in need if such services are not provided.
The plan goes on to underline who should get help from the CAP. Persons who benefit from assistance and welfare services include children who are in care or in need of protection due to abuse or neglect, mentally and physically disabled persons. I have many mentally disabled persons in my riding. The provincial government under then Premier Davis decided to deinstitutionalize the programs for the mentally handicapped. That was a good program but it did not come with any support services. It turfed them out on to the streets, and these persons are out there with no supervision as to when they should take medication, no help with housing and so on. The provincial Conservative government abandoned them and now the federal Conservative government is abandoning these people who are in need. Then there are one-parent families, the aged, the unemployed. Let me share what is happening with the unemployed in the Toronto area, specifically in Parkdale-High Park. People with university education are losing their jobs. They are going on to the unemployment insurance rolls. When their UI finishes they have no choice and are forced on to the welfare rolls.
Every time I meet with the chairman of metropolitan Toronto, Alan Tonks, and the newly elected mayor, June Rowlands, they are saying that the federal government is abandoning its responsibilities to the provinces and to the municipalities.

The CAP is to help the families or individuals in crisis. This is left up to the Salvation Army because the federal government has abandoned these people. Then we have low income workers and battered women. Most of the men in this House wore white ribbons last week, and what happens this week? The government is going to implement Bill C-32 to cut programs for battered women. One week they wear white ribbons; the next week they cut the programs. That is the sincerity of this government. It is no wonder the public is losing faith in such management and in such ruling.
Every day we see headlines of how the cap on CAP is affecting people. Turning to medicare, every day we see headlines such as: "Budget Crunch Puts Care Jobs at Risk" and "Hospitals Face Crisis".
The Toronto Star.

No, it is not The Toronto Star. That was The Ottawa Sun, for the minister's information. They continue: "Bed Closings in Hospitals to Increase, Langdon says". Here is an item from a Tory paper, The Globe and Mail: "Ontario says hospitals may have to merge", "Minister warns of tough times ahead", "More lay-offs are inevitable, hospitals told", "Hospital squeeze", "Cash strapped province insists on belt-tightening".
This has nothing to do with transfer payments.

The minister says: "This has nothing to do with transfer payments". It has everything to do with transfer payments.
Now the effect of transfer payments hits education. My daughter just began university this year. The professors at the university are warning the students already that their tuition fees next year may go up by 20 per cent to 30 per cent.
May.

May. Let us not pass this bill and then they will not. The minister says: "May". There are other students who went to the same high school as my daughter and are not in university because they could not afford it. What a shame. Students with talent and potential cannot go on to university because of this federal government saying nyet to education. Yet the same government puts out a $20 million package called Prosperity Through Competitiveness.
Government Orders
My daughter tells me the first programs that will be cut at the post-secondary education level will be languages. How can we stand up in this House and say we are going to promote competitiveness? We want to be more competitive, but we cut off the languages. We are not going to speak the languages of the countries we are going to trade in. What an investment. What mismanagement.
My God, get your act together, you people on the other side. If you are going to put millions of dollars into talking about competing and being more competitive then do not cut language programs in the universities.
My daughter, Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
I believe the hon. member should be accurate. Education is a provincial responsibility. Those decisions are made by the universities and by the provincial governments, not by the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, that was not a point of order and I believe that should be pointed out.

I want to go back to dealing with our universities. My daughter is studying French.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, how they teach French in universities? They put 100 to 200 students in a class. They give them a French textbook and they tell them to translate it into English. That is the way we teach French in our country. Instead of having small groups of 20 to 30 students so that they can learn, they are given a textbook and are told to translate. Why are they using those methods? It is not the fault of the professors and the universities. It is because the federal government has been cutting these payments and they have to stick 100, 200 or 300 students in a language class.
Good Lord.

That is what our education has been debased to. This same government wants to teach and spend millions of dollars so that our students will be competitive in the future. It dismantles post-secondary education and then it supports its advertising and consultant friends in order to give them jobs. Will my daughter get a job when she finishes university? She will not be able to speak the other official language the way it is being taught in the universities right now.

When I read the headlines I see another shocker. Another effect of Bill C-32 is how the transfer payments are going to affect the police. The Ontario Provincial Police is very worried. There are headlines such as "Provincial Police Face Lay-offs as a $16 million Deficit Looms", "Cutbacks Hamper Police Work, OPP tells the Solicitor General", "Budget Cuts Threaten"-

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of this amendment put forward by the NDP. I am happy the Minister of State for Finance and Privatization is in the House today. I do not think he is focusing on something happening in the marketplace today which is as much a part of the economic equation of managing a country as looking after things such as fighting inflation and making sure we have a lower interest rate.
It has to do with the spirit that exists in this country today. I want to say to the minister that I recognize the interest rate is the lowest it has been in 18 years. I recognize that the inflation targets for the government are probably three or four months ahead of schedule.
Inflation in this country is practically zero. Reducing inflation is a noble objective. No one in this House would argue that point. However, the aggressive, lean, mean approach that the government has as its agenda has caused a fear factor in the marketplace today. This has caused an incredible drag in terms of the consumer confidence and spending habits.
The people out there without jobs, and even the people with jobs, are fearful they are next to go. When we hear of corporations like IBM and Dialects Diversified, institutions that are foundations within our community, going through a restructuring it is natural that it sends a shiver into the marketplace.
I talked with one of the local fruit merchants on the weekend. He runs Sunland Fruit on the Danforth. He was telling me that people are buying more and more damaged goods. In other words, a sale one or two years ago might have been $20 or $30 but now people are buying $5 or $6 worth of fruit because the fear factor is so high. They are only buying $10 worth of fruit at a time. The fear factor has really taken hold of the economy.
One of the instruments the government has to stabilize the marketplace and minimize some of that fear is the CAP. The Canada Assistance Plan was always meant to be a secure safety net. The 5 per cent cap on it is a symbol. Most Canadians do not understand. In other words, it exacerbates the fear factor.
What do we hear from the provinces and municipalities? We hear about all these programs, whether they are for one-parent families, the aged, the unemployed or people on welfare. Because the unemployment insurance fund has been cut back we now have many more people on welfare and we have a problem in terms of the welfare system being properly funded in terms of battered women and low income earners.
When we hear that the government is putting a cap on the Canada Assistance Plan it exacerbates the fear. In other words, are things that bad in our country that the national government is sending out such a signal to the most disadvantaged people in our society?
Earlier today we talked about the motion the hon. member put forward dealing with a national heritage day. One thing this country in terms of its heritage has had great pride in, in the last few years, is our strong social safety net.
One instrument is the Canada Assistance Plan. Even if times are bad it is one of those instruments that we do not tamper with because it sends the wrong signal into the marketplace. It exacerbates the fear factor and puts a drag on consumer spending, which is ultimately going to affect all our retailers and to cause a never-ending vicious circle in terms of our unemployment and other social services. For so long we have had absolute pride in these services and have had a sense of security that we would never tamper with them.
My point to the government is that it is sitting over there way ahead of the inflation targets. It is sitting over there with an interest rate that is the lowest it has been in 18 years, but it must also realize that one of the reasons the interest rate is so low is that the consumer spending is almost at a standstill.
I would suggest to the government that it is time to park this lean, mean machine type approach and put a little of caring back into its economic plan. I do not think anyone in this country would argue with this government's ability to be a lean, mean machine. Part of
December 9, 1991

governance is also having as part of its value system an attention to caring. I think that on this bill it should go back to its caring factor and drop this cap on CAP.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood said that no one would argue with the characterization of this government as a lean, mean machine. The minister was quick to point out that perhaps the Reform Party might argue with that characterization. I think it is instructive that as lean and as mean as this government has been, the Reform Party would promise to be even more Tory than the Tories, which is something people who might be considering voting for the Reform Party should keep in mind. If they do not like what they have received from this government, it makes absolutely no sense to vote for the Reform Party which would give them an even heavier dose of what is afflicting them now.
This cap on the Canada Assistance Plan which is the way in which the federal government has traditionally cost shared social assistance programs with the various programs, is a despicable moral as well as economic choice of action. What we see here in the cap on CAP is really the government's ethical framework being revealed for all and sundry. At the same time as it refuses to consider eliminating the business and entertainment tax deduction which goes toward the financing of lunches for the rich and famous and special hockey seats for friends of corporations, et cetera, it is keen to put a lid on the assistance that goes to people, many of whom must now use food banks.
At the same time as the government is still willing to finance through the tax system very expensive lunches at very expensive restaurants, it is limiting the ability of those Canadians who must now use food banks for their lunches to further their own economic interests and perhaps at some point get themselves off social assistance.
The government also refuses to consider eliminating a number of other tax loopholes, such as the interest deductibility rule which is used by foreign corporations to borrow money here interest-free so that they can expand their operations elsewhere; the manufacturing and processing tax credit which was variously justified over the
Government Orders
years in ways that no longer hold water but still continue to exist; the special tax treatment of capital gains; the special tax treatment for real estate developers for writing off depreciation on properties that technically are supposed to be depreciating but are actually rising in value.
There are others such as the 21-year deemed realization rule for the trust accounts that were set up in 1972 which the government has indicated it will change so that those wealthy families that 21 years ago put this money aside will be able to continue receiving that tax break.
All these things stand out in contrast to the cap on CAP whereby this government has said that when it comes to touching the rich, its policy is to make things better for them. The Minister of Finance said clearly in one of his speeches in this House that Canada does not have enough rich people. This government has certainly gone out of its way to ensure that the rich in Canada feel better than they did previously. It has changed the income tax system, which used to be more progressive than it is now, so that the top few per cent of Canadian income earners pay even less tax than they did before.
These are indisputable facts. The Minister of State for Finance can argue the contrary if he likes, but the fact is that his government did so amend the progressive income tax system that the people in the very top bracket now pay less tax than they used to. That is a fact that even the government is not willing to dispute because it was part of an intentional policy on its part.
What we have here is the contrast between what this government is willing to do for the very wealthy in Canada and what it is doing to the very poor in Canada by extending this cap on the money it is willing to make available to cost shared programs with Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. The reason initially given for this was that these were the three wealthiest provinces and they should be able to carry this burden by themselves.
There are two things wrong with that. First, we do not unilaterally break a federal-provincial agreement that has existed for decades. The Canada Assistance Plan is a program which after many studies has been found to be, although not perfect, one of the best federal-provincial programs in the country.

Government Orders
The government is unilaterally withdrawing from this as it is from other federal-provincial programs. It is no wonder we have a constitutional crisis and a lack of confidence in the federal government. The government has taken upon itself to do all these things unilaterally, to pull out of agreements that it made years ago.
Unfortunately for the hon. member for Broadview- Greenwood and others who may have spoken to this amendment, this had its origins in Liberal governments. It was a Liberal government in 1982 that first unilaterally changed the federal-provincial fiscal arrangement when the Minister of Finance, now the hon. Senator MacEa-chen in the other place, unilaterally changed the federal-provincial fiscal agreements that were to be negotiated in 1982.
I do not say that to excuse the other side because it has certainly accelerated that trend. It criticized it when the Liberals started it, but it no sooner got into office than it was guilty of its own unilateral action. There was action after action after action of this type, whether it was with regard to Established Programs Financing or Canada Assistance Plan or, for that matter, other programs.
The fact is that what we have here is a trend line of federal governments getting out of agreements in a unilateral way. Unfortunately, as I say, that was started by the Liberals but it did not need to be accelerated and made much worse by the Conservatives.
Ontario and other wealthy provinces are in a very difficult position, Ontario especially right now because it has that many more people going on social assistance thanks to the free trade agreement. It is radically restructuring the economy of Ontario in such a way that there are not the kinds of jobs there used to be.
I was just reading an article the other day about how some 36 or 40 per cent of people are on social assistance in Ontario now. These people had very good jobs not so long ago, only months ago. It is a real problem for Ontario. It is very bad timing for the government to say, at a time when Ontario is going through such difficult times thanks to the free trade agreement: "Sorry, you are going to have to go this on your own even though it is a federal government policy, the Canada-U.S. Free
Trade Agreement, which has created the situation in Ontario".
All in all, this is a truly despicable act by this government. Putting a cap on CAP and now extending it is a sure sign of the ethical depravity of the government on the other side which chooses, as I said before, to put limits on traditional commitments to helping the poor in Canada while at the same time refusing to close these many tax loopholes which continue to benefit the very rich.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, listening to the last speaker provoked me to rise and say something because he spent the bulk of his speech, as the members of the New Democratic Party are often wont to do, attacking the Liberal Party's record in terms of its dealing with recessions in this country and talking about the fact that the Liberals are ones who started to cut some of the transfers to the provinces.
If he would listen to what I have to say, he might learn something. Clearly his attempts at blaming past Liberal governments for this are misguided. First of all, he forgets that Liberal governments established the programs in the first place. They are the ones that set them up, not the Conservatives and not the New Democrats. The New Democrats have never had office in this country and they have not set up a thing. It is the Liberal Party, when it was in government, that set these programs in place in the first instance. For the member to sit here and dump all over the Liberal Party in the course of his speech is frankly ridiculous.
The second thing is that he should remember how NDP governments behave once they take office. We are seeing it every day in Ontario. We realize what a disastrous situation people in our province face. It is a serious crisis in Ontario, and it is more serious because of the fact that it has an NDP government which seems incapable of dealing with the situation.
One only needs to look at the vast increase in the provincial debt which is not being used to create new jobs. It is being used to pay people to do nothing. That is what the Ontario government is doing. It should be spending its money on capital projects as Liberal governments have done in the past.
My hon. friend from Broadview-Greenwood knows extremely well that in the last recession the federal
December 9, 1991

Liberal government spent billions of dollars creating jobs in Canada by funding capital projects across the country.
They spent money they did not have.

The hon. member says: "They spent money they did not have". I agree that they did that, but the proper course is to borrow money and spend during the course of a recession and that is exactly what they did.
This government has continued to borrow through six years that it says are the best Canada ever had. The hon. member for homelessness says that is not so. The six years they have been boasting about as being years of unbounded prosperity in Canada and which the Prime Minister keeps talking about are the years in which they have continued to run up Canada's debt $30 billion a year.
Thke credit for it.

The hon. member says: "Take credit for it". I am reluctant to take credit for his government's incompetence. He knows perfectly well that his government has bungled this thing so badly it does not know which way to look. He is embarrassed now. He is starting to blush. I can understand that. He should be blushing furiously at the way his government carries on.
This is the way the Liberal Party in the past has carried on: it created and paid for capital projects to create jobs in Canada and to put Canadians back to work. Sure they increased the deficit to do it but any economist knows that is the normal practice. You spend in the tough times so that you save in the good times. The difference is that this government failed to save in the good times. It kept increasing the deficit and now it is in a position where it says: "We do not want to run up the deficit further in order to create jobs".
Then we have the NDP government in Ontario which runs up the deficit fivefold and does not create any new jobs. You know perfectly well it has not created any new jobs.
That is hypocrisy.

The hon. member says this is hypocrisy. He knows what is going on in this country. He knows how his government has failed to get the deficit under control through six years. Here we are almost into year eight of Tory mismanagement and the national debt has doubled,
Government Orders
thanks to his government he has supported throughout. That is why the government is unable to deal with the crisis it has created in Canada through its economic mismanagement.
The New Democratic Party government in Ontario is now offering peanuts to people who are on welfare. It is not able to keep up with inflation rates. After standing in this House complaining constantly about how fair the NDP is and how unfair any increase of less than inflation is, it seems once it takes office it starts acting like Tories. We have always suspected that the NDP and the Tories were in bed together. I see members opposite are laughing. They should be ashamed, not laughing. Even the minister is starting to blush again. It is a shame.
In any event what I want to deal with is the unfairness of this bill. I suggest that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex-Windsor is a reasoned and sensible amendment. This bill is a bad bill. It should not be approved by this House in this form or in any form.
The cutbacks the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park mentioned in his speech are real. They are keenly felt in my constituency of Kingston and the Islands. The cuts in education have been a disaster. This federal government, by making these cuts, has made it more and more difficult for the provincial governments to maintain their share of educational expenditure that is so vital in our country.
This competitiveness paper that the government is spending $25 million on is a great waste of the taxpayers' money, yet the government is so keen on indulging in it. It recognizes the need for education as a high priority to make Canadians competitive in the global environment it says is so important and is so much a part of the situation Canada is facing. Instead of assisting in education expenditures it cuts them. It cuts them in what it calls the most prosperous provinces, the have provinces of Canada, where the money is needed as much as any place else in this particular rubric of public expenditure.
If we cut funding for training and education in Canada, how are Canadians going to compete in the global environment the government says is so much a part of our system? Surely to goodness we have to continue those expenditures. We have to augment those expenditures, not cut them. This is particularly so at a time of recession when the provincial governments, including

December 9, 1991
Government Orders
the NDP government in Ontario, seem so keen on cutting expenditures to post-secondary institutions.
I was just reading in the paper the other day how the minister of education in Ontario is warning the universities and hospitals to expect a zero increase or a very low increase this next year. How can we cut funding to our educational institutions which are the backbone of our future competitiveness if we are going to put ourselves in a position where we are competitive? It defies all logic and it defies all reason.
That is the policy that is being pursued both by the New Democratic Party in Ontario and by the federal Conservative Party in government in Ottawa. It spells a disastrous potential consequence for the people of Ontario and the people of all Canada if we pursue this kind of blind and wrong-headed policy that is inappropriate for the circumstances which are based on all the government's other reports.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I also smile at the harangue from my colleague who just sat down. It is very clear that the Liberal Party shifted dramatically to the right after its Aylmer conference. Now of course it is trying to put up a big smoke screen. Its members are the ones who initiated the national debt because of their mismanagement of the economy. Many of the things that we are now seeing in the cutbacks to social programs were in fact initiated and promoted by the Liberals when they were in government.
It is quite interesting to talk about Bob Rae. He is now 4 per cent or nearly 5 per cent more popular than he was the day he got elected.
No, he is not. Check the polls.
The polls show he is well over 40 per cent elected as of last week. He is very popular and it is time the Liberals started taking a look at that.
What hypocrisy.

It has been very clear that his government has the support of the people because they understand many of the things it is doing. Let us take a look at the Canada Assistance Plan and what it was designed to do.
It was designed to deal with poverty in Canada and its causes and its effects on people. It was designed to deal with a whole range of welfare services from day care to child abuse to services for battered women. These are the programs that are now being attacked by this bill and by this government.
The Canada Assistance Plan was based on a federal-provincial partnership. It was a concept that called for the federal government to be involved with the provinces in these kinds of programs. I think it is very important to remember at a time when there is anguish in this country as to whether there is any reason to keep the country together that the government has been attacking these unity programs that are based on a partnership between the provinces and the federal government.
We have to start to make the conclusion that many Canadians are now questioning the validity of Canada because of the tax on these programs.
I want to focus a bit on the whole issue of income assistance. The income assistance case loads in most provinces are up dramatically for two reasons. The first is the change to the unemployment insurance scheme which makes it more difficult for people to qualify. They are entitled to income assistance for a shorter period of time. The second is the recession in this country. It has been deliberately precipitated by the federal government through its free trade deal which has devastated the industrial heartland of the country.
I guess that is what caused the recession in the States too, is it?

The high Canadian dollar and the artificially high interest rates have certainly wiped out many of our export industries including the lumber industry in British Columbia. They are still too high compared with those of the United States.
The federal government creates these things by changing unemployment insurance and by the recession. Then what does it say? "Of course we do not want to have to meet the financial responsibility for these kinds of changes. What we are going to do is pass legislation, offloading the responsibility on to the provinces, particularly the three big provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario".

It simply limits its liability to 5 per cent at the same time as it is dumping down on to the provinces not millions but billions of dollars of expenditure. Of course it has impact. It has an impact even on large provinces like Ontario. It cripples the province's ability to provide for the poor.
It is also starting to do a couple of other things. It is undermining some of the fundamental concepts within Canada. One of the things that happened when the Canada Assistance Plan came in is that residential requirements were waived. One could move from one province to another province and be entitled to receive financial assistance or income assistance.
I remember when I first started working in public welfare in British Columbia. A whole bureaucracy was designed to track down not only the province but the municipality in which that person lived for one full year without receiving any public assistance. Then that person had to bill back the municipality and the province for the income assistance that was granted. A whole bureaucracy developed.
All of a sudden now the wealthy provinces are hearing: "If people come from Nova Scotia, from Manitoba or from Quebec, we are not going to cost share". People are now starting to say: "Maybe we should get back to the old idea of residential responsibility. A person's financial assistance is the responsibility of the province in which they last resided a year".
Without financial help from the federal government, provinces are being forced to say: "Maybe that is what we are going to have to do". All the things that this Tory government does destroys standards of national programs. In income assistance it said that one could not use residential requirements in order to restrict income assistance.
I think it is very dangerous for the government to single out individual provinces for differential treatment particularly when it comes to social programs. Then it is simply saying: "We are going to treat you differently from other areas".
Another whole area of the Canada Assistance Plan relates to family violence and child welfare. This is the most hypocritical area in which this government has functioned. It champions the whole UN year of the child and the rights of the child and then refuses to live up to it. The government makes a big announcement about the program on family violence spending $137 million spread over five years. Actually it will spend some $40 million
Government Orders
before 1993 when it is going to be long out of government office.
Then what does it do? It takes back from those provinces three and four times the amount of money they could have used for child abuse prevention and investigations of child abuse, for battered women's shelters, for transition houses and for counselling programs for women who have been abused. These are all of the very basic programs that are necessary to stop family violence. The government guts with its limit on the Canada Assistance Plan but then does a great PR splash saying: "We are going to solve it with this money that we are going to spread out over a number of years".
The Canada Assistance Plan is one of the mechanisms that has a unifying effect on Canada. This government has chosen to attack it, as it has attacked other types of unifying and social programs.
The government must no longer be surprised that this consistent attack results in the questioning of the unity of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have decided to partake in this debate this morning because of the number of comments that I have heard from the other side of the House. I would like to try to put a few things on the record.
I found it interesting when the NDP member for Essex-Windsor was up talking this morning about Ontario and how difficult it was. I am confused because I am not sure where he is coming from. On Friday, he was up defending the budget of the Ontario NDP. As a matter of fact, he was quoted in Hansard on page 5947 as saying: "It is striking that the unemployment rates have continued to go up in every other province but have decreased in the province of Ontario thanks to the excellent budget that was put into effect in that province".
On one hand, when he was here on Friday, he talked out of this side of his mouth, but when the debate goes the other way, he is talking from the other side. The member knows that.
The other thing that I think is important on these programs, and one of the difficulties, is that the federal government in a cost sharing program is responsible for paying 50 per cent of the costs. Yet we do not have exact firm controls as to how the money is spent. As a result,

Government Orders
sometimes provinces will spend money and then send the bill to us afterward.
I would just like to quote something that was in the Ontario NDP budget of this year. It said: "Total payments from the federal government were $406 million higher than the forecast in the 1990 Ontario budget. Part of the increase was for prior year claims while most of the increase reflects significantly higher levels of provincial spending on cost shared social assistance programs".
We are asking to put controls on it, but that is how it works. It was reflected in the Ontario budget. I am standing here quoting this morning from NDP pearls of wisdom that have been stated both in Queen's Park and here.

I represent an area that by national standards is considered one of the most affluent. I had the occasion, along with community leaders, organizations and associations concerned with individual Canadian's needs in my area, to participate in a report called Addressing the Crisis of Human Services in York, Region.
Today I stand in the House of Commons, look to the government side and analyse what it has done with the present state of the economy. I soon realize this government has obviously lost touch with the reality of what is going on in this country. It has lost touch particularly in the area of caring and compassion.
In my area, the report that I cited earlier clearly indicated that of all the times to be cutting transfer payments to the provinces, this is the worst.

We are faced with a situation where we have single mothers and people who are suffering and calling out for help. Addressing the Crisis in Human Services in the York Region in one of its recommendations calls for the federal government to work to increase the level of federal assistance to cost share human services programs.
