Let me tell you, there are people hurting and in poverty, and need sees no boundaries in this nation. What people want from the federal government is the type of leadership that will bring effective change and reach out to those people who are desperately in need.
We have 1.5 million Canadians unemployed who need help. We have single mothers who are compelled to stand with their children in front of their local food bank for their daily meal. In an area as rich and affluent as the York region, the Fire-Fighters Association, the Salvation Army and I were forced this year to have a food and toy drive.
The Conservative agenda does not work anywhere in this country. It does not work because it fails to realize that one of the most fundamental purposes of governing and government is to reach out to people when they are in need.
I want to go back to the report in the York region because we have been seriously hit by the regressive economic strategy of this government. We have seen a widening gap between the rich and the poor. We have seen an unfair tax system. We have seen during the boom years a government that accepted all the extra revenue. Now Canadians are asking why it has not been able to get the deficit and the debt under control, while at the same time Canadians have been whacked over their heads with unprecedented tax grabs.
There is an accountability problem with the federal government and people in my riding of York North and elsewhere are asking themselves how this government is dealing with communities like mine that have a high population of young families. There is an increased
demand for schools, child care, family counselling and health care. They want to know from this government what it is going to do with York region, which is the fastest growing municipality in the greater Toronto area. It has the lowest per capita community mental health funding in the province. York region's Children's Aid Society has the lowest per child funding in the province. The education system is the fastest growing in the province of Ontario and schools are over-enrolled on opening date. York region has one women's shelter, one men's hostel, eight group home beds for homeless youth and it is the third lowest funded public health unit in the province.
This is all happening in the perceived land of the rich. There are people in my community who are hurting. I think the response we are getting from the federal government is not the one that I, as a member of Parliament, can accept. I do not accept it because I think the federal government has a moral obligation and a duty to reach out and not merely accept things as a fact of life. Because 1.5 million unemployed Canadians should not be a fact of life in an industrialized country like Canada.
We should not merely accept human tragedy and family breakups as something that occur in every day Canada. I remember when this nation offered Canadians opportunity. I remember when this country gave young people the type of hope that was required to build a prosperous nation. Today we are devastated by bad news. Today we are demoralized by a government that only cares about taking care of the few, the friends of the government, while it is punishing millions and millions of Canadians with inaction. It is watching them as they cry out for help.
That is not the way we have governed in the past. That is not the way Liberals governed. While this government uses a tunnel vision approach toward the deficit, it is doing it on the backs of the unemployed. It is doing it on the backs of single mothers. It is doing it on the backs of those individuals who need help the most.
I will tell you that Canadians will not forgive this type of attitude. They know best when their children go starving, when single mothers and single parents are lining up in front of food banks every day of the week. Canadians are sick and tired of this type of arrogant attitude that is bringing about the demoralization of Canadians from coast to coast to coast.

I ask the minister, who is attentively listening to what I am saying, to force cabinet to start looking at the human side of governing instead of looking at a bottom line that is creating despair, and not caring about those individuals who are truly in need.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to speak against Bill C-32, or more particularly to speak in favour of our amendment. It would cut out clause 1 of Bill C-32 and have the same effect as defeating it.
Bill C-32 is not only a cruel bill that will affect millions of people who are in deep trouble through no fault of their own. It is also a very foolish bill and furthers what this government has already done to destroy the economy of Canada.
In round figures, this bill will probably cost the governments of British Columbia and Alberta $389 million in their 1991-92 budgets. In Ontario, it has cost $415 million in the 1990-91 budget and $1.2 billion is expected to be the cost in the 1991-92 budget.
Figures like that are so large that the average person listening has a hard time telling the difference between a million and a billion. If they get a few thousand in income in a year, that is the size they are familiar with. I want to talk a little bit about the effects.
The former finance minister brags that he will be taking more than $2 billion per year now out of the people of Canada through this cap, this lid he has put on the Canada Assistance Program. This is the only program through which Ottawa aids the neediest people in the provinces of Canada.

Their programs for the young people, the children, the youth and the young adults are being chopped because the grants on which they have relied are being cut back or wiped out. Mr. Speaker, this bill to limit the growth in federal payments to the richest provinces to 5 per cent and the amendment moved by
the finance critic of the New Democratic Party to simply maintain the status quo reflect the lack of debate and a minimum consensus in the country.
Canada Assistance Plan spending grew much faster in the richest provinces in the last 10 years and federal transfers to the richest provinces grew much more than those to the poorest ones. This has intensified since the Progressive Conservative government took power in 1984.
In fact, federal transfers for the Canada Assistance Plan and even all federal transfers to the provinces increased more rapidly for the richest provinces than for the poorest ones, even if equalization is included.
Since 1984 federal transfers to the poorest provinces rose at a 5.7 per cent rate, while those to the richest provinces went up 7.7 per cent. Taking out equalization, which offsets this somewhat, the growth rate for federal transfers to the richest provinces would be almost double.
Today we have a proposal from the federal government to limit transfers to the three richest provinces to a 5 per cent growth rate, and the New Democratic Party, which claims to defend the poor, is opposed and brings in an amendment that would simply cancel this bill. That party, which should defend the poorest provinces, on the contrary clearly seeks to maintain the status quo of federal transfers favouring the richest provinces.
That same party very recently raised a hue and cry because of the regional development agreement whereby the federal government would give Quebec $160 million over five years, or a little more than $30 million a year. In equalization payments alone Quebec has lost $2.2 billion since 1987. For the current year, the cuts will amount to some $440 million. Did you see a single New Democratic member rise to denounce the situation? They all get up this morning to denounce a bill that would restrict the growth in spending in the richest provinces.
That is the real face of the NDP, and I hope Quebecers will take a good look, because this morning, they had a chance to restore a modicum of fairness to transfer payments. I agree this is a unilateral decision by the federal government, whose power to change unilaterally the rules of the game in fiscal arrangements has just been confirmed by the Supreme Court. It is also a

situation that is intolerable for any responsible provincial government. Fiscal arrangements should include a mutual commitment by the federal government and the provinces that any changes in these arrangements will be negotiated. We would have a good chance to get a more balanced system, now that fiscal arrangements between the provinces and the federal government must be renegotiated for 1992-1997, and in fact, negotiations are under way. However, there has never been any serious debate about the type of fiscal arrangements, the type of agreements we want to see between the federal government and the provinces. We are now seeing a transfer of the federal deficit to the provinces, and unlike what is being said today about the New Democratic Party, these cuts, these transfers have, in recent years, tended to concentrate on the poorer, not on the richer provinces.
The freeze on transfer payments for health care and education applied to all provinces. The capping of equalization payments has been in effect since 1987. Yet we had to wait until 1991 for a cap on spending by the richer provinces which are still getting more funding from the federal government, funding that should be used to establish some kind of balance, to restore a measure of fairness and maintain the fiscal ability of governments to provide services to the entire population. This situation is so obvious that the finance ministers will meet this week, when the Government of Quebec will again clearly express its views on cuts in equalization and EPF transfer payments but also on the money the federal government wants to raise. I did not hear anyone from the NDP mention this. The new taxes that the federal government will raise through its decision to no longer allow deduction of payroll and capital taxes for federal income tax purposes will cost Quebec $46 per capita a year and Ontario $15 a year. Alberta and British Columbia will gain $39 and $16 per person respectively.
Not only are transfer payments cut but the tax base is being reorganized in such a way as to collect $325 million more. In that context, the bill presented by the government this morning is a small measure of fairness towards the provinces with less fiscal capacity, while the system as a whole is still very beneficial to the richest provinces.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. He puts the argument about the impact of this bill and the successive policies of this government on national unity exactly where they should be put.
This bill that puts a cap on Canada Assistance Plan contributions to three provinces in Canada is a divisive bill. It penalizes those who can afford it least. It further destroys the social service network in this country and represents in my submission a very serious blow to national unity exactly at the wrong time in this country's history.
Bill C-32 which we are now dealing with at report stage extends from 1992 to 1995 a specific limit on federal contributions under the Canada Assistance Plan to three provinces: Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. Its predecessor Bill C-69 put a limit on caps to 1992. In the last budget the government announced its inten-
Government Orders
tion to proceed with this legislation to extend the cap to 1995.
The financial impact of this bill is very significant. The government has said it expects to save the federal treasury $2 billion a year and it seeks to justify this bill on the basis of financial constraints on the federal government.
This bill is flawed for three broad reasons. First, it is attacking the deficit by going after social programs which will inevitably have a negative impact on those who can least afford it at a time in our country's history when we are facing recession right across Canada.
We hear for example that in metro Toronto there will be over 200,000 children this Christmas who will have to get Christmas dinner at food banks. Child poverty is one of the disgraces of this wealthy nation. This bill will perpetrate and extend the scandal in the way in which our society has treated our children. This comes after the words of the Prime Minister at the UN not so very long ago who spoke at a summit on the rights of children.
We have rhetoric and no positive action. The only action we get is a bill of this kind which will have a direct impact on children and those who can least afford it.
The second problem with this bill is that it fails to attack the deficit where it should be attacked. The deficit that has built up in this country over the last 20 years by successive Liberal and Conservative governments has been almost entirely as a result of two policies by both Liberals and Conservatives. The first policy has been to give increasing numbers of tax breaks to the corporate sector and to wealthy individuals. A recent study demonstrated that 44 per cent of the current deficit is a result of those policies started by the present member for Vancouver Quadra when he was Minister of Finance. This continued under successive Liberal governments and has been given an accelerated drive by the Conservatives.
The second policy which both Liberals and Conservatives followed whenever the economy got into any kind of trouble was to increase interest rates. We saw it in the early 1980s when interest rates went up to over 20 per cent and we have seen it recently under the Conservative government. This of course had an impact on the deficit because as the federal government was beginning to run into deficits each year, the accumulated debt required

The third problem is with the impact of this bill on national unity. Let me speak to that in particular. First of all, this bill breaks a specific agreement with the provinces. This was a unilateral breaking of an agreement with the provinces.
The courts have found that this Parliament is within its jurisdiction and the government is within its legal right to bring forward this bill. But we submit that it has no moral right to introduce a bill of this kind which breaks a solemn undertaking that had been given to the provinces across Canada.
Second, the bill discriminates against three of the ten provinces. It has picked the so-called have provinces. These are the ones which also have large bills for social assistance because of the recession which the government has imposed on this country. It develops an argument whereby it says: "This does not affect us. We cannot therefore have any problem with adding to the tax bill of the people of Ontario, Alberta or British Columbia". It is a bill which gives a reverse kind of
special status to B.C., Alberta and Ontario. At this time in our country's history it is a bad bill.
Finally, it very specifically attacks our social security and social service system. This is part of a larger Conservative agenda and is at a time when that very social service system is one of the distinctive natures of our country and is a key foundation of building a sense of nationhood.
The Canada Assistance Plan is a plan which is effectively a federal-provincial partnership. It has been in existence for many years. The federal government undertook to pay 50 per cent of the cost of designated social services at the provincial level. This gave the federal government a large and significant role in the social security net in this country. This represents a significant step by the federal government to back away from a federal role in social services in Canada. It is part of a larger agenda of which this is a key part.
First, this government has changed the tax system in order to reduce the burden on the corporate sector and those of wealth.
Second, this government through the free trade agreement has reduced protections for Canadian industry and opened this country up to even greater attack from multinationals from outside the country.
Third, this government has made it easier for foreign companies to attack and invest in Canadian companies and to buy Canadian companies even with our own money.
Fourth, the government has set about a process of privatization which has undermined public institutions.
Fifth, it has been an attack on public servants in this country and Public Service employees in particular. We saw the recent attack on the Public Service employees in the PSAC strike. We have seen a set of policies, including contracting out and including the use of exclusions and designations to undermine collective bargaining at the Public Service level.
When even that failed, the government came in and passed legislation to impose its own agenda as an employer on Public Service employees in Canada.
Most critically, it has attacked social services in this country. It has attacked family allowances and pensions. It has gone after medicare and accessibility of university and higher education in this country. It has reduced the effectiveness of unemployment insurance which has again imposed a special strain on social assistance programs right across the country.
December 9, 1991

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Your time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak out against Bill C-32, the Canada Assistance Plan and the 5 per cent limit to the provinces of B.C., Alberta and Ontario.
I would like to start out by making a few comments with regard to the speech made by the Bloc Quebecois member. I think he made a very interesting speech about his concerns, but I want to say to the member from Quebec that if you are poor in Quebec and you are poor in the Atlantic provinces and you are poor in British Columbia, then that is what this plan is all about.
We should not be starting to bring in legislation that is going to start to bring about caps in some provinces because they happen to be rich. The poor in the provinces across this country are crying out for help. We have a national program that is supposed to be the Canada Assistance Plan.
I say to all of you what a time to be discussing the Canada Assistance Plan. It is three weeks before Christmas and this government is bringing in a policy that is going to cap social assistance programs in the province of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
I say it is shameful. I say to the people in the food banks across this country as the people line up there that some of these government members better go down to those food banks and listen to what is going on across this country. I want to say to you that you would not be bringing in a cap at this time for these people across Canada.
At the same time, as my colleague for Juan de Fuca has said, the banks are making profits with their credit cards and various things. We have raised this in this House and the government turned a deaf ear to it. It does not want to hear that. It does not want to hear that the banks are making a profit. Why can we not bring in a taxation system that when a worker makes his wages, he is taxed immediately on his wages and on what he does. Why can we not tax the banks and the large corporations at the source of their profits at 20 per cent minimum tax as the hon. member for Juan de Fuca has said. "We
should bring in a minimum tax across this country". The Liberals would not do it. The Conservatives sure are not going to do it. The New Democrats will soon show the people of Canada a fair taxation system. The NDP will bring about a fair taxation system that will recognize the needs of the people of Canada.
We will not do it by dividing the country. We will not do it by cutting back on social programs. The Prime Minister of Canada in the last election said that our social programs are sacred to the people of Canada and to this government.
Mr. Speaker, I see my time is running short so I will continue after Question Period.
It being two o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday a letter from the minister of fisheries was printed in the Charlottetown Guardian. In this letter the minister said that because the lobster fishery is the biggest fishery in Prince Edward Island, Island ground fishermen did not deserve government assistance.
For the last 18 months fishermen have been calling for their fair share of government assistance.
In the recent $40 million aid package, Prince Edward Island did not get one cent. In the $584 million package in May 1990, P.E.I. received a miserly $150,000 from the government, some of which went to study the GST centre in Summerside.
I challenge the minister of fisheries to listen to the inshore ground fishermen who will not be able to make their boat payments. I challenge the minister to explain to fishermen why the ground fishery in P.E.I. does not get help.

December 9, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I rise today because I am concerned about the future of my country, also because I am concerned about the recent comments on this nation's future made by the leader of the Parti Quebecois.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, on many occasions the concept of our country has been described as a marriage. The people of my constituency believe that this country like a marriage is an association created out of mutual love, trust and respect. Any other concept is nothing more than a common law relationship.
The people I represent are not interested in a common law relationship for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we continually hear the Prime Minister saying how proud we are to be Canadian citizens. However, this undoubted privilege is being denied to some 50,000 legal immigrants who are now trapped in an Order in Council backlog.
For these tens of thousands of immigrants, who by and large have completed their security and health checks and are in Canada, this backlog is the only thing that stands in their way to becoming landed. They must receive their landing papers before they can apply for citizenship.
There is no reasonable explanation for this delay. The reality is that the government is holding them back so that the immigration levels announced by the immigration department can appear as though they are being met.
I ask the government to stop playing with figures. These people are here in Canada and have been processed in accordance with our laws. There is no reason to delay their landings any further. It should stop playing with the numbers because by doing so it is playing with people's lives.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to congratulate the Yukon Territorial Government, the Council for Yukon Indians and the federal government on reaching an historical aboriginal selfgovernment agreement.
The agreement ratified by four Yukon First Nations this past week signals the end of one era and the beginning of a new relationship, a relationship based not on dependency but on equality. The agreement puts into practice the principle that Yukon's First Nations people have the inherent right to govern their land and their people.
It shows all of us that when the political will is there, when governments of all levels can come together and there is a genuine commitment to creating a more equitable society, self-government can be achieved.
I strongly encourage the government now to ratify this historic self-government agreement and put principle into action.

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, December 18, there will be a forum in the town of Springhill, Nova Scotia to address a proposal by Dr. Bruce Filiter for English speaking Canadians to indicate their desire to keep Quebec within the country.
Dr. Filiter believes the politicians have not been successful in delivering messages back and forth between Quebec and the rest of Canada, and I agree with him. He also believes that unless ordinary Canadians begin to show each other that they care about the future of the country we have a distinct possibility of losing it, and I agree with him.
Dr. Filiter's idea is that English Canada could send a very clear message by flying the Quebec flag at every opportunity, and this will be his proposal put forth at the seminar on December 18.
In a letter to the premier of Nova Scotia he has said that flying a Quebec flag may be a small gesture but it is gestures like this that can smother the flames of separa-
December 9, 1991

tion fanned by the misunderstandings and petty jealousies and the media's preoccupation with divisive forces.
I agree with Dr. Filiter that it must be up to Canadians from all walks of life to stand up and be counted in this debate. The politicians and the media have done a very poor job in sending messages back and forth and have certainly exaggerated any differences there may be.
I applaud Dr. Filiter for his efforts and determination and wish him every success in his approach to this all important question.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, December 8, was the fiftieth anniversary of the beginning of the Japanese attack on Hong Kong which ended on Christmas Day of that year, 1941. Of 1,975 Canadians, 557 were killed or died in prison camps. Those who returned after years of brutal treatment would never be the same.
Their will to live and their will to be good Canadians, in spite of doubts about the wisdom of the policy and the government that sent them there, should be an example to all Canadians who are tempted to cynicism about Canada by much less personally devastating events.
The Canadians at Hong Kong were Winnipeg Grenadiers from Manitoba and Royal Rifles from Quebec. Let what they did together in defending the indefensible and in suffering the insufferable put our current tribulations into perspective and remind us of what Canadians can do as Canadians when the best in them is called to the fore.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Minister of Transport, officially announced the creation of the Val-d'Or airport economic development board.
The new agency, made up of community representatives, is meant to promote and develop the interests of this northern Quebec regional airport. Transport Canada's regional airport in Val-d'Or boasts a runway that is
10,000	feet long and 200 feet wide. It has already accommodated a Concorde, Boeing 747s and the USAF Galaxy C-5, the world's largest plane.
Today, the airport can handle 400 to 500 flights a day and up to 30 flights an hour. Last summer, international airlines started making technical stops in Val-d'Or. A feasibility study showed that a market for technical stops exists on east-west routes to Toronto and Chicago.

Mr. Speaker, this evening in St. John's two events are taking place at the Radisson Hotel. In one the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans from Newfoundland and the Prime Minister are engaged in a function inside the hotel at $500 a head. At the same time another function goes on, a soup kitchen. That one is at the hotel, though outside. It is a soup kitchen to serve some of the poor who have been hurt by the policies of this particular government.
The two events are together a graphic summation of what is happening to this country: while some people hobnob at high prices and dine luxuriously, the other half who have been decimated, whose jobs have been lost by the policies of that same elite, sit outside in the cold and eat soup at 50 cents a bowl.
My one disappointment is not that the minister of fisheries is celebrating 25 years. I congratulate him. He has done some good service to the province and to the country during those 25 years. What disappoints me, though, is that tonight he will find himself inside the room with the elite instead of outside with the people who sent him here in the first place, a place where he is often much more comfortable. I appeal to him at this late hour to stay outside instead of going in with his buddies, the elite.

Mr. Speaker, in a free and fair referendum on December 1, the citizens of Ukraine voted for freedom, democracy and independence.

Yesterday in Winnipeg hundreds of people gathered at city hall to celebrate by raising the Ukrainian flag. One of the speakers of the ceremony was Mr. Ihor Derkatch, member of Parliament from Ukraine. Other guests included representatives of the Ukrainian Orthodox and Ukrainian Catholic churches and speakers from all levels of governments representing all political parties.
Canada was the first western country to recognize the independence of Ukraine. It is quite clear from declarations made by the Ukraine Parliament and from statements made by the new president, Mr. Leonid Kravchuk, that Ukraine will be a strong advocate of international arms control and human rights.
It is therefore imperative that Canada further recognize a free Ukraine by establishing diplomatic relations immediately.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday the government announced in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal a major green plan initiative to combat smog. This initiative should result in significant reductions in emissions of nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, the main smog creating pollutants, and will lead to a major improvement in air quality over the next 10 years.
Specifically new regulations, protocols and codes of practice will be developed for rail transportation, vehicle diesel engines, power and chemical plants, and dry cleaning facilities. A research program will be implemented as well as a public education campaign, and bilateral agreements will be negotiated with the provinces.
This green plan initiative is a major step forward in our fight against smog in this country.

Mr. Speaker, there are disturbing reports in today's papers
that the government is backing off its commitment to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act to include sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination.
In 1986 the government accepted the subcommittee on equality's recommendation that the Canadian Human Rights Act be amended to include just such a prohibition.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission has also repeatedly recommended that the government amend the act. Human rights codes in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Yukon all include such protection.
The government has the responsibility to protect Canadians who face discrimination. Further, the government has a responsibility to live up to its promises. There are many Canadians who suffer from discrimination on account of their sexual orientation and require protection. It is unacceptable for this situation to continue any longer.
I urge the government to act without further delay and introduce the long delayed legislation.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday I took part in a ceremony commemorating the first anniversary and completion of renovations to Woodstock Sanctuary House. This project was made possible on funding obtained from the federal government through CMHC's Project Haven initiative.
Woodstock Sanctuary House provides temporary accommodation to victims of family violence. The transition home operates on a 24-hour per day basis to provide shelter, food, emotional support and access to other services. It also provides a safe and secure refuge to abused women and their children.
Woodstock Sanctuary House recognizes the specific and distinct needs of children from abusive environments. Congratulations and a thank you are in order to the citizens of Woodstock, New Brunswick and surrounding communities for working to make Woodstock Sanctuary House a reality.

Mr. Speaker, almost eight years later this government still has not managed to lay the foundation for a prospering economy. The current recession shows no sign of turning around for the better. So far this recession has a casualty toll of 71,000 lay-offs in Ontario, and last year alone 350,000 jobs disappeared permanently in Canada.
With businesses continuing to fail, thousands of Canadian workers are becoming the permanently unemployed. Welfare rolls are skyrocketing and families are relying on food banks to make ends meet.
Ask any retailer: the Christmas boom has turned into a Christmas bust. Canadians are displaying their lack of confidence in the Canadian economy and their lack of confidence in the current government.
When will this government stop pretending there is a recovery and start doing something about this dragged out recession? The Prime Minister even makes Scrooge look good, if that is possible.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are suffering from chronic constitutional fatigue. They are tired of debate, sick of threats, weary of consultation, and fed up with rhetoric. Constitutional dialogue cannot be a one-way street. It is time traffic moved in both directions.
The Meech Lake process did not fail in June 1990. The spirit of Meech was destroyed in much of English Canada in December 1988 with the passage of Bill 178 in Quebec.
I want to congratulate Premier Bourassa and the Quebec Liberal Party for their resolution yesterday calling for alternatives to Bill 178.
Quebec and its people are an important and valued part of Canada. It is time for its leadership to come to the table and get involved. Yesterday's motion concerning Bill 178 is a most welcome step in this direction and indeed should be applauded by all Canadians.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
The Minister of State for Finance bragged on Friday that his government was expecting a good recovery and that it was already under way. However the figures show quite a different picture. Last month alone the Canadian economy lost 49,000 jobs. Statistics Canada noted that
305,000	manufacturing jobs have disappeared forever since June 1989.
The only benefit of this economy seems to be the U.S. retailers who pocketed more than $3 billion from Canadian shoppers. People have given up hope. They are disappearing into the black hole of jobless despair.
Does the government intend to base its so-called recovery on simply sweeping Canadians under the carpet?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows full well that in the second and third quarters real growth averaged 3.3 per cent, an increase of 3.3 per cent. It is a modest increase in growth but it is growth and we do feel that we are coming out of the recession.
For the hon. member to describe whether I was bragging or not, I certainly did not mean it in a bragging sense at all. We are still in tough economic times, but we are coming out of them.
The hon. member should do a little promoting about Canada rather than talking about people travelling to the United States to shop. It would do us a lot more good.

Mr. Speaker, what we on this side of the House would like to do is promote food for hungry children.
The number of people depending on food banks in this year of so-called recovery has increased by 20 per cent. Some 284,000 kids will depend on food banks this Christmas. To put it in perspective, we could fill the SkyDome, B.C. Place, and the Olympic Stadium with

Oral Questions
hungry children and we would still have 100,000 kids waiting outside trying to get a meal.
These kids are not sitting on Santa's knee asking for presents. They want food and they want a government that will care about them.
How can they call it a recovery when the line-up at food banks has increased by 20 per cent this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nobody takes comfort in seeing families in need at any time of the year, but especially at this time of the year.
To be fair, the hon. member knows full well that a number of people, low income families, have come off the poverty roll over the last period of time. We know that we have increased the child tax credit. There are a number of projects that this government has undertaken to help those who need the help at this period of time. Of course the low income rebates from the goods and services tax which pays cheques quarterly to low income families is also a source of aid at this time.
I wish we could do more. I think everyone in the House wishes we could do more, but in this period the best thing for these people and for all people in Canada is to ensure that our economy gets back on track, that jobs are created, and that people are able to get off unemployment insurance and welfare and back into the work force with a meaningful job. That is our goal and we are going to accomplish it.

Mr. Speaker, in Montreal alone there are 50,000 needy children, almost enough to fill the Olympic Stadium. We also know that Robert Normand said on Saturday that he expected unemployment to rise to 11 per cent. How can the government claim that the recession is over when it knows that the number of needy children has risen 20 per cent this year alone?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was the same question in French as it was in her English supplementary.
I can tell the hon. member that the economy is picking up. It is starting to improve. It is a vested interest for opposition members to see poor conditions because they
think that will vault them into power the next time around.
Let me say to the hon. member that the economy is getting better. If we talked a little more positively about the good things in this country the economy would pick up faster, instead of the whining we hear time after time from the opposition in this House.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
A confidential report of the Department of External Affairs says that for competitive reasons Canada must never lead the world in the development of environmental standards.
This is totally contrary to the Porter report, to the competitiveness strategies of Japan and Germany, countries which have already stated that being ahead environmentally is an integral part of their plans for economic dominance.
My question is: How could this government introduce an economic prosperity agenda a month ago and obscenely spend some $21 million, spreading it cross the country, when its true agenda is to deny Canadians the opportunity of becoming competitive in the fastest growing market of the next decade, that of the development of environmental technologies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the hon. member wait until he can read the entire report.
I would like to mention first of all that my colleagues, the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of State for Environment and I just met with some Canadian leaders from the Stockholm conference who are helping guide us toward UNCED. One of the things we have been discussing is the important connection between trade and the environment and how we indeed can use environmental issues.
We are into a different world now than we were before. The two go together. We are proud of our environmental record in Canada and we intend to

continue to stay in the lead on environmental issues in the future.

Mr. Speaker, unless the minister is now in the process of busily rewriting the report, I have the complete copy, and it is very clear that it says that Canada must improve its step, must not lead our partners in the development of environmental standards.
The statement on the government's strategy is not only bad environmental policy; it is incredibly dumb and archaic economics.
However, be that as it may, my supplementary question is: How does the minister reconcile the statement in this strategy paper that in terms of environmental protection Canada must not move ahead of its trading partners, with the contrary position that has been taken by the same government that in the North American Free Trade Agreement it is perfectly acceptable that Canada enforce environmental standards that are much higher than that of Mexico?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the pertinent part of the document the member is referring to when it will be made public is the objective sections of the document. That is the one the hon. member and all members of this House should look to. I pray that he will wait until that document is out and then he will have the benefit of looking at the objectives part to make any judgment or statement about this document.
Furthermore, the hon. member made an allusion to the fact that environmental technologies are important. This government, through the green plan, announced a $100 million initiative.
That is nothing.

Only a Liberal would say that $100 million is nothing. Over six years $100 million for environmental technologies is what is dedicated through the green plan to develop technologies and bring them to the marketplace. That is the commitment this government has made.
In the context of the Canada-United States-Mexico trade agreement, the hon. member also knows that we are conducting parallel negotiations with the three parties on environment issues. That is something that in
Oral Questions
itself is unparalleled and has never been done before. We are making great progress in this area.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. Today we heard that housing starts are dropping, that cars are not selling-20 per cent fewer cars were sold this month than last month-and that stores are expecting business to be slack over the holiday season. The economy is crumbling and during this time the Prime Minister is travelling across the country to raise funds for his party and his ministers responsible for the economy are busy with the Constitution. When will this government set its priorities straight and help Canadians find work?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, housing starts are at an annualized rate of some 174,000 which is about the average over the last number of years for Canada. They are up some 20 per cent over last year's starts. Those are hopeful signs.
As far as car sales are concerned, the hon. member said that sales are down 20 per cent. One of the interesting things is that foreign sales are down rather dramatically and North American made cars are up about 1.5 per cent. That is not a great increase but at least an increase. Those are workers for Canada not for the foreign makers.
Those are good signs we are seeing in the economy. We hope they will continue.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
We would all like to see good signs, but a 13 per cent decrease in housing starts and the sale of vehicles being down 20 per cent are not good signs either to the people who sell, to the people who manufacture or to the construction workers.
I want to say also that 35,000 manufacturing jobs were lost last month alone. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association said: "If job losses continue at this rate we have only got 30 months left before no one is left".

December 9, 1991
Oral Questions
I want to ask the minister: When can we expect an announcement of a first ministers' conference on the economy and a clear indication that the government will take such a conference seriously and be open to changes in its economic policies?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has been meeting with provincial premiers across Canada and the Minister of Finance will be meeting with the finance ministers this Thursday to discuss many of the issues that the hon. member raises and that the premiers have raised with the Prime Minister.
Once those meetings take place on Thursday and Friday, the Minister of Finance will be in a position to advise the Prime Minister on the advisability of having a first ministers' conference on the economy.
I would point out the comment of Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa when he said that he would consider going to a national summit on the economy if other premiers do not turn it into a concert of whiners. We want to make sure that that is the case.

Mr. Speaker, I have another supplementary question.
While Canadians would like to see some action by this government on jobs, we still have a million and a half unemployed, the same number on social assistance or unemployment insurance, and hundreds of thousands of children who can expect to find their Christmas dinner, if they can find it at all, in a food bank. At the same time the banks in this country are still posting almost $4 billion in profit this year.
The minister knows there are loopholes that will allow banks to avoid paying taxes on much of this profit. The government says it needs money. The people of Canada know that money is needed. Is the government prepared to take action so that the banks will pay their full and fair share of taxes this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member raised that question, because indeed before this government came into power banks hardly paid any tax, if any at all. Last year they paid three-quarters of a billion dollars in tax and this year they will be paying more than double that amount. There are taxes coming from the profits that the banks are making today.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Finance.
He pointed out that on the weekend the premier of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa, became the sixth premier to express a willingness to attend a first ministers' conference on the economy.
I ask the minister or the Deputy Prime Minister: Now that a majority of premiers are interested in having such a conference, why will the government not announce today an early first ministers' conference on the economy so that the federal government can work with the provinces to create new economic growth and more jobs for all Canadians? What is it waiting for?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the hon. member did not hear my answer to the Leader of the New Democratic Party. I will repeat it for him and I will go slowly so he can understand it.
The provincial premiers across the country have met with the Prime Minister and they have given a number of agenda items that they would like to talk about.
The ministers of finance are meeting on Thursday and Friday with the Minister of Finance of Canada to discuss agenda items on a number of the subjects that the provincial premiers wish to discuss.
Once those meetings are over the Minister of Finance will give the appropriate advice to the Prime Minister in co-operation with the provincial premiers. There is no sense announcing a meeting today until the ministers of finance have had an opportunity to discuss these issues, as well they should.

Mr. Speaker, while this minister is responding with callous arrogance to the concerns we express on behalf of the million and a half Canadians out of work, more and more of them are being added to the welfare rolls.
In its recent proposals on the Constitution, his government said it wanted to work with the provinces to strengthen the economy.
I ask the minister how his government and its proposals can have any credibility with Canadians when just two months later the federal government has not expressed a willingness and in fact so far is refusing to meet with the

very provinces it said it wanted to work with to keep the economy moving? Why does this government not have any real commitment to economic growth and jobs for Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just ask the rhetorical question: What do you think the finance ministers are meeting about this week? What a silly question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
In April 1989 this government announced the creation of a Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies. Last March the commission mandate was extended by a year. Last week for perhaps the first time ever, appointed members of a royal commission announced that they were suing the same royal commission in the Federal Court.
How could this government let things get so out of control? Why the gross mismanagement of such a serious matter?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies is dealing with very complex issues regarding research into the reproductive system. You get into surrogate motherhood, sperm banks and organ transplants. They are very difficult. We look forward to the recommendations that the royal commission will bring forth at the end of 1992 and know that they are overcoming some very difficult issues.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the chairperson of the standing committee on health and welfare.
Twenty five million dollars has been spent by this commission and now this commission refuses the medical community for summaries of the commission's funded proposals. Will the chairperson of the standing committee on health and welfare convene a meeting of the standing committee so that members of Parliament
Oral Questions
of all political parties may question and probe the commissioners of this incredible fiasco.

I just want to make it quite clear that provided that question is strictly directed to what the committee is about to do, the hon. member can answer it. The question was directed to the chairperson of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, we are having a business meeting of the committee tomorrow. I would certainly be interested in discussing the issue there. I am not certain that the subcommittee on the status of women is the most appropriate venue for such a hearing, but I certainly do think that there should be a hearing on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, may Canadians believe that the elimination of the GST would be a great boon to the Canadian economy and bring us out of the economic doldrums that we are in.
The Minister of Finance said just last night on TV that the money raised by the GST would be difficult to replace.
I ask the Minister of State for Finance: If the government is truly interested in alternatives to the GST why the government refuses to consider eliminating the business entertainment tax deduction, the special tax treatment of capital gains, the special tax breaks for real estate developers, tax breaks for mergers, interest deductibility for foreign owned multinationals, the manufacturing and processing tax credit, the dividend tax credit, just to name several many billions of dollars that the government could look at if it was serious about the deficit, instead of its ideological agenda?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find it passing strange that New Democratic Party members who stand up here, as their leader did today, and complain about jobs disappearing in the manufacturing industry would absolutely cripple that industry with additional taxes.

Mr. Speaker, what is crippling the manufacturing sector in this country is the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement brought in by

Oral Questions
this bunch over there and the fact that they refuse to admit it.
If the government is serious about deficit reduction, as it always says it is, why does it refuse to consider eliminating all these tax loopholes that are benefiting wealthy Canadians while poor people have to line up at food banks on the same day that the government is putting a cap on social assistance in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to make a blanket statement like that, one that it is just helping wealthy Canadians, is nonsense.
The various tax incentives that are there are designed to make our Canadian industries competitive with their competitors with the United States and other countries with which we compete.
Certainly we have got to compete with them. We export 35 per cent of what we produce. We have to be competitive. If we followed the NDP policy on taxation, we would be taxing our industries completely out of the competitive field and we would be wiped out by the people whom we have to compete with in other countries.
The tax measures that the hon. member refers to are not tax loopholes. They are tax incentives, and he knows that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Acting Minister of Transport.
At the end of last week, the Minister of Transport indicated in Winnipeg that the government is now seriously examining closing the port of Churchill in the new year, a decision that would have a disastrous impact on the prairie economy and certainly upon the town of Churchill itself.
I want to ask the minister why, when there have been a number of recent grain shipments to the various republics in eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, a portion of that grain cannot be shipped through the port of Churchill. Why is this government engaging in a
conspiracy with CN Rail to shut down the port of Churchill?
Mr. Speaker, there is no conspiracy with CN Rail to shut down the port of Churchill.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 CROATIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to seek leave to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 52 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the unfolding tragedy in Croatia.
The federal Yugoslavian army continues its unrelenting attack against Croatia and has resumed shelling of Dubrovnik. A recent report of the European Community monitors has documented widespread and unprovoked attacks against civilians, hospitals and schools.
Finally, on November 18 this House did have an important debate on this question. I hope that the House would agree once again to debate this issue to look at the very serious situation, including the possibility of the immediate sending of UN peacekeeping troops and the question of Canada's recognition of Croatia and Slovenia.
Government Orders
I hope the House would agree to an emergency debate tonight on this desperate situation which affects the people of Croatia and about which all Canadians are deeply concerned.
