The House resumed consideration of Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance; and of Motion No. 1.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak out against Bill C-32. I am resuming my debate begun prior to breaking for Question Period when I was discussing what the Prime Minister had said during the last election and during the free trade agreement. He stated that the social programs were sacred and that he would see they were kept sacred in Canada.
Of course we have a bill here that brings about a 5 per cent cap for British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario. That is not bringing about a universal system.
I want to say that during the free trade agreement when these kinds of discussions were taking place and they were talking about the level playing field, these were the kinds of issues we tried to bring before the Canadian people, what this government would be doing.
I want to refer a bit to some of those programs and how it is affecting them. This government brought in the free trade agreement shortly after we came back to the House. After all the profits being made by the banks we have Bill C-21 which makes it harder to get UI and makes it run out more quickly.
Again we have the government bringing in Bill C-21 which will change the whole system. In the past the

Government Orders
workers, the employers and the government shared equally in contributing toward that program. Now the government has brought about a change which eliminates its participation in that program. It is strictly an employee-employee relationship. This reverts directly to the free trade agreement, so that it can say to the Americans that it is not subsidizing this program any more.
Then we go to another act that came into the House dealing with the partial deindexing of family benefits. It means families that need money get less each year. This is another program to show its American friends that it is not going to be subsidizing these programs.
The clawback of family allowance and pensions, also partially deindexed, means that the threat of cut off of benefits gets higher each year. Again the government can say to its American friends that it is looking after this and bringing about an order that brings about a fairer playing field.
There have been further cuts to social assistance, to health and post-secondary education. Bill C-69 and Bill C-20 are threatening the future of medicare and accessible education. Again we come right back to the free trade agreement because that is what is happening. This government is systematically bringing about changes to the programs in Canada to tiy to meet the needs of its American friends.
There is still no sign of the long promised national child care strategy which is so desperately needed in Canada. There is no mention of that during these times.
We have the high Canadian dollar which the former President of the Treasury Board in the last government told the Canadian people was directly related to free trade. The high Canadian dollar was promised to the Americans to offset the kinds of markets we were going to be dealing with.
That high Canadian dollar in Kootenay East has affected our coal sales and our national sales, because it is all tied to the Canadian dollar and how we sell our mining materials. We have had those kinds of problems throughout and they directly affect our social programs.
The GST is directly related to the free trade agreement. What we have seen here is a system of programs brought about by this government to implement its free trade agreement.
The Prime Minister promised the Canadian public that the free trade agreement would not affect our social programs. The Prime Minister said it was a sacred trust. I say the Canadian people cannot trust this government or the Prime Minister to look after our universal social programs. They are under serious threat. We must stand up in this House and defend those programs at every opportunity we get.

Mr. Speaker, the convention on the rights of the child was the main topic of the UN summit on children co-sponsored by Canada on September 29 and 30, 1990 in New York City. I understand that Canada will be adopting the convention for ratification some time this week.
The summit for children made a declaration which was very progressive, very compassionate and very far-reaching for the children of the world and for the children of Canada.
Unfortunately the rhetoric of the government does not necessarily come out in its legislation. We have before us action being taken by the government which indicates that its sincerity in the summit a year and half ago in September and the ratification which is coming this week are mere words. It is not taking the same kind of action for the children of Canada.
One of the government's actions relative to children is this Bill C-32 which puts a limit on the amount of increase the federal government can or will make to the Governments of B.C., Alberta and Ontario relative to the Canada Assistance Plan. The Canada Assistance Plan is basic legislation in the country which was set up to alleviate poverty and support things like the Canada Health Care Program.
If you are poor in Alberta it hurts just as much as if you are poor in Newfoundland. Poverty is always hardest on children. All this discussion about the summit and the convention of the rights of the child is so much rhetoric when you allow children in this country to live in poverty.
For example, one child in six in Canada is poor. There are over a million children under the age of 18 in Canada who live in poverty, making children the largest single group of people living in families on low incomes.
Does the government think that none of these children live in Quebec, Ontario or Alberta? Almost half the number of Canadians who rely on food banks for something to eat part of the time are children. Approxi-
December 9, 1991

mately 284,000 children go hungry and need to go to food banks to eat. An article in The Globe and Mail says:
As many as 284,000 children in Canada won't have enough to eat this holiday season, a spokesman for the Canadian Association for Food Banks predicts. Gerald Kennedy, who is also the director of the Daily Bread Food Bank in Toronto, said that this estimate is based on the number of households receiving social assistance and relying on the food banks.
There are 50,000 children who go without food part of the time and need to use food banks in Montreal. We could do that kind of liturgy for every one of the large communities across the country.
The government keeps telling us that there are less poor in the world or in Canada lately. Although there has been a decline in the number of children living in poverty in Canada since 1984, there are still more poor children than there were 10 years ago, despite a 3.7 per cent decline in the total population of children in Canada. As if Bill C-32 is not damage enough, we have gone through another series of bills over the last few years which has contributed to the poverty that children live in or the difficulty their parents have taking care of them.
As my colleague has mentioned, Bill C-21 makes UI harder to get and it runs out more quickly. There was a partial deindexing of family allowances and of old age pensions. The clawback of family allowances and old age pensions which have already been partially deindexed means that the threshold for cutoffs of benefits gets lower each year.
There have been further cuts for social assistance and for health and post-secondary education in Bill C-69 and Bill C-20. These bills threaten the future of medicare and accessible education.
This kind of legislation contributes to the malaise that is felt all across the country. It also contributes to the poverty, the need for food banks and the need for more assistance. This bill suggests there is a need for more assistance to these kinds of situations but that need is not in Ontario, Quebec or Alberta.
We are dealing with the problem of disunity in Canada and we are contributing to this kind of disunity by treating some provinces differently. Bill C-23 is another attack by this government on the social programs the
Government Orders
government claims it is doing in the name of fiscal restraint.
Fiscal restraint depends on how we spend the money or where we get the money. The government is getting its money from the poor who are the people who need it most. It is allowing the banks to increase their profits by over $137 billion this year. It is not taxing them anywhere near the level that they are taxing the poor. If those banks paid 7 per cent tax on that amount just like we do on every product we buy, we would get a lot more taxation from the banks.
My colleagues and I will not support Bill C-32.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to rise in opposition to Bill C-32.
Our party has been in the forefront of opposing this legislation when it came to the House earlier in September. I thank my many colleagues who rose at that time to keep the debate going. We opposed it during the budget. We lead the way in opposing it during the committee hearings. Many groups came to us and they had the same perspective as the Liberal Party in that not only do we oppose Bill C-32 but we also oppose Bill C-20.
Those who are interested in looking at the record will notice that last week one member after another rose on amendments and on a major motion to protest to the government about the declining support for health and social welfare.
This week I was struck by two more developments. The first was the articles in the newspaper about the increase in the number of people who use the food banks, particularly for children. As we head into winter I am struck by the number of times we see nothing but negative articles about this. I was fortunate to visit the Soviet Union. I saw the bread lines forming throughout the Soviet Union, particularly in Russia. You say to yourself: How can that country survive the lack of food? You come back home and you look not at the same scale but at the same phenomena. We can no longer feed our youth. We can no longer care for the people who have turned to us for years.
I was struck by the report coming out of Nova Scotia from the Nova Scotia working committee on the Constitution. In its report entitled Canada: A Country for All there is a discussion of social programs on page 28:

Government Orders
Nova Scotians are of the view that our social programs must be preserved, protected and promoted across the country. This includes universal hospital and health coverage, unemployment insurance and all the rest of the net of programs which guarantees a level of assistance to all Canadians.
Interest was also expressed in extending that net through changes like a guaranteed annual income. Other people are worried about the consequences of the changes that are taking place at the federal level.
Let me just say that that paragraph in a capsule expresses the concern about social programs and the implications of bills such as Bill C-32 are not those of the whimsical interests of the opposition parties. In fact they are at the heart of the concern being expressed across the country.
The damage has not only been done by the federal Conservative Party. One of the ironies is that the provincial government in Ontario last week was unable or unwilling-this is perhaps a better word-to contribute to those people on social assistance who so desperately need support. I am sure the member for Kingston and the Islands would have noticed this since it is his province.
According to testimony in front of the committee on finance last week, over 900,000 people in Ontario are now on social assistance. According to some reports, over 250,000 of those people live in metropolitan Toronto.
Here is the jewel of our country being destroyed federally by the Conservatives and provincially by the NDP. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands knows that. One of the saddest things is that in the narrow partisanship of the NDP in this debate, they refuse to address these national issues.
They refuse to understand that the question of tax reform permeates not only federal but provincial governments. They join the ranks of the provincial premier who for endless generations attacked the federal government looking for a scapegoat.
Here we have now the new Messiah in Canadian politics, the premier of Ontario. What does he do? He chooses to attack the federal government. It is an easy way out, but you must be committed to reform across the board and wiling to chastise your colleagues when the time comes to chastise them.
The Liberal Party which is more experienced in governing knows full well how to chastise its colleagues when time comes.
Tell us about the provincial Liberal government which left us a deficit of $8 billion.

The member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan said the Liberal government in Ontario left "us" a deficit of $8 billion. He said: "us", the royal "we". Here we have a voting member of the Ontario legislature joining us. He has a dual appointment. What an anomaly. It is us or them. There was that whole speech by the last member. It is us or them. Tax the rich. Save the poor. It is a great new speech. I have not heard that for 200 years.
What is it with these guys in their analysis? They have not read anything for 200 years. They have no understanding of the changes going on in Canadian society. They have no understanding of how to fight for Canadians. Instead they stand up with these cliches in the House hoping to fool their householders with no understanding of the damage that they are doing.
A good example is standing there.

The member is throwing some support. That is very kind of him. A multipartisan approach in this thing would be greatly appreciated.
I stand up decrying the misuse of the House for partisan points and wishing that all members would understand that it is the responsibility of all levels of government to help the poor.
I oppose Bill C-32 because it shows the inability of this government and the unwillingness of this government to fight for the poor of this country. I decry those other governments when it takes a mandate on one premise, then turns around and governs on a different premise.
I know parties who have always criticized the Liberal Party: "You campaign from the left but you govern from the right". We are seeing across this country people manipulating and voters given the hope of a better future and it turns around and treats them more miserably than the last government.
It is a shame but one that should be spoken about in public so that all Canadians understand this debate that is taking place.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that the bill before us in its timing as it winds its way through this House and on to the other
December 9, 1991

place is a very lousy Christmas present for the poor people and the lower income people of this country.
During my short intervention I want to give an indication of what we are up against. I want to talk about my own community to let you know what the impact has been of the economy brought to us by the Government of Canada.
There is the high dollar, the higher interest rates although they are coming down, which is a plus, and the free trade agreement. We have seen mills close entirely. We have seen work forces at paper mills cut in half. We have seen the woodlands operations almost disappear. One company is planning on making them all but disappear because of the change in operations.
We have seen an increase in general welfare assistance. The number of beneficiaries has gone up by almost 19 per cent from September 1990 to September
1991.
We now have 3,767 beneficiaries in the community of Thunder Bay with a population of about 110,000. Our social services department estimates a 56.4 per cent increase in general welfare assistance expenditures for 1992 over 1991.
We have to recognize that the Canada Assistance Plan is a formula that at one time ensured that provincial governments and municipalities could afford to deal with the fluctuations as the numbers of welfare beneficiaries rose or dropped.
We now find that in Thunder Bay our gross costs in 1992 will be $28.5 million to look after the people in our community who have no jobs, who have no unemployment insurance, who have no disability payments and who have no pensions in order that they can get by in a very meagre way.
We are seeing signs in other areas. There are ramifications from this kind of playing with peoples' lives and peoples' futures. The Lutheran Care community in Thunder Bay provides for people who come in looking for help. In 1991 they gave out 755 hampers up to September or about 84 a month. It is interesting to look at the breakdown of the income source of these people: some 44 per cent are general welfare recipients, 20 per
Government Orders
cent are on family benefits, 9 per cent are on disability income; 12 per cent are unemployed, 12 per cent are the working poor and 3 per cent are transients. This is some society we have where people on government income assistance still have to rely on churches and church organizations and community organizations to get by from month to month.
The Do Drop Inn is a soup kitchen operated by St. Andrew's Roman Catholic Church in Thunder Bay. It serves about 80 people a day. That is up 30 per cent from last year. Fifty per cent of their clients are psychiatric patients who have been deinstitutionalized. They were turfed out into the streets without any kind of support whatsoever.
At this time of year when we obviously tend to think of others less able or fortunate than us, we find that in Thunder Bay we are expecting that 2,600 hampers will have to be produced for the Christmas cheer fund to be delivered to 3,900 children and 2,100 adults. That is 6,000 people who need the assistance of charity in order to get by this Christmas. I do not think that is the kind of society we want. By capping CAP we are contributing to that situation in our society.
In our emergency shelter, there has been a 40 per cent increase in 1990 over 1989 and another 18 per cent increase this year. In 1991 they averaged 75 people per day at the soup kitchen.
When the Government of Canada through the first bill and now through Bill C-32 decided to put a cap on the province of Ontario, the province of British Columbia and the province of Alberta, they in effect decided that if you are poor in Ontario it is different than being poor in Atlantic Canada. If you are poor in Alberta, it is different than being poor in Saskatchewan. If you are poor in B.C., it is different than being poor in the territories.
Surely this government understands that you are poor no matter where you live; if you do not have enough money to put a decent roof over your head or to wear clothing appropriate for the climate that we have or to purchase the kind of food that an individual and family needs to get by in a healthy way. Poor is poor is poor. The government says to Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia that it is going to slow down the money coming into their provinces because they are have provinces. I cannot

Government Orders
speak for Alberta or B.C., although I know that times are tough there as well, but I can tell you that in Ontario we have been ravaged by the recession. We have been ravaged by the free trade agreement brought to us by this government. We have been ravaged by the high dollar that has seen thousands of jobs across the north disappear, not just temporarily but forever. We have been ravaged by the changes in unemployment insurance, so those people who do have a good severance package find their income eroded because of the UI regulations and legislation. We have been devastated by the softwood lumber fiasco that this government allowed to happen. Sawmill after sawmill is closing, woodlands operations are closing and people who have no other skills, who rely on the Canada Assistance Plan to get by, are thrown on a waste heap.
I am the first to admit that money made available to welfare recipients and to anyone on income support, by federal and provincial governments, is insufficient today to meet their needs. There is no question about it. The federal government is saying to Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia that they have to do more on their own. It is not going to help them as much. By saying that, the government is telling the people of Ontario, Alberta and B.C. it does not value them in the same way it used to. It does not care if they are hurting. It does not care if they have massive increases in unemployment and welfare rolls. They have to find their own funds.
In previous governments, both Liberal and Conservative federally, when money slowed down from the federal level to the provinces, the provinces found themselves having to transfer the responsibility down to the local level. Provincially and federally, revenues primarily come from income tax, while at the local level it is user fees or property taxes.
Municipalities can no longer afford any increases. In some ways the federal government is transferring its deficits to the provincial level. The provincial levels find themselves shifting the deficits to the municipal levels. It is all the same taxpayers. They all have had enough of this game playing. They are crying out for some kind of fair tax system to ensure that services are provided to those who need them when they are needed in a quality way, without putting people on the streets and cutting
back on programs for income assistance, child care, community services support and what have you.
That is why my party has always opposed this bill. That is why we will be voting against this bill. It is wrong, wrong, wrong, just like this government is wrong, wrong, wrong in almost everything it does.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is really quite unfortunate that we are dealing with this legislation, Bill C-32, legislation to put a cap on CAP, the Canada Assistance Plan.
At this date, the House moves toward its adjournment at the end of the week for the Christmas time period. Most Canadians are hoping that it will be a festive season, when in fact the government of the day is the grinch of the day. Canadians will find lumps of coal in their Christmas stockings from the Conservative government this year as in the past couple of years.
It is amazing as well how much damage a government can do with a bill that is two pages long. The legislation we have been debating lately is 300 to 400 pages long, is very complicated, amends a great number of bills and requires a great deal of concentration and scrutiny to see exactly what is being done.
Today it is different. In two quick pages, this government is doing more to try to destroy social programs in Canada than the 400 page bill that we dealt with just the other day. It is important to really put on the record some of the concerns and problems that we have on this side of the House, certainly in the New Democratic Party in any case, over this legislation.
Let us have a little bit of background. "The Canada Assistance Plan, which was enacted in 1966, had the objective then of encouraging the further development and extension of assistance and welfare services programs throughout Canada by sharing the costs of such programs with the provinces and territories". That is official. That is from the Minister of National Health and Welfare in a letter that he wrote to me when I expressed my concerns about Canada Assistance Plan funding and the various programs and how they might apply in my community, primarily the Prince George area.
The result of this government's more ideological view of the world is its concern for Canadians and its drive to

really put that Conservative imprint on the social policy in Canada, a policy that is failing in Canada.
There is no question that when you talk to Canadians in each province, you will find that people are rejecting the Conservative view of the world and we are all hopeful that in the election which will come either next year or the following year, Canadians will ensure that they follow through with their vision of what Canada should be at the ballot box and send a strong message to the Conservative Party.
This legislation, which allows for the extension of the 5 per cent limit on the Canada Assistance Plan in B.C., Alberta and Ontario, as my colleague from Thunder Bay said, means you are different if you are poor in Ontario, British Columbia or Alberta. You are different there because this government has decided that those provinces are not deserving of the ongoing commitment to social assistance and social programs that the federal government should be providing.
The very provinces being affected by this legislation from the government are the provinces that likely are going to be in the greatest need of the Canada Assistance Plan. When the economy is failing as it is, because of the GST, because of free trade and the other economic measures of this government, it is these provinces that traditionally in our country have been seen as the provinces in which if you lose your job somewhere you can go to these provinces and try and find other employment and what have you. Unfortunately for many of the people in our country, they end up on assistance, be it in British Columbia, my province, or in Ontario in which the municipalities even have to share in some of the costs.
It must be an incredible burden for some of these local governments in Ontario, given the devastation that free trade and the tax policies of the government have wrought on that province.
The Canada Assistance Plan is an important and integral part of the kind of programming we have put together in this country, the shared vision of Canada between the federal and provincial governments. We have the Canada Assistance Plan, a 50/50 sharing program with the provinces. We have the Established Programs Financing focusing primarily on post-seconda-
Govemment Orders
ry education and health, which is suffering, as I have raised in this House many times. We have the block funding formula which was started by the Liberal Party and now allows some provinces to spend health and education money on highways. We have the equalization formula.
We also have a number of specific federal-provincial agreements which help develop the economic aspects of our country and provide for the different social programs such as forestry in British Columbia. Our agreement there fell far short of what was required. Nova Scotia, as another example, is still waiting for the minister of forestry to actually sign the agreement with that province, though he tells the forestry committee that he hopes that maybe before Christmas some of the ministers who want to get in on this can all get their date books together and find some time to actually sit down and sign on the dotted line, so to speak.
This Canada Assistance Plan plays an important role. It is a vehicle through which the federal government works with the provinces and in some cases with local governments to deliver social assistance programs.
I have done some research in my own area of Prince George.
I have a list of some 20 organizations that are registered by the government as societies that can benefit from this: Mums and Kids Drop-in, Native Friendship Centre, the YM-YWCA, the Home Support, Senior Citizens Activity Centre, Spruceland Parent Participation Nursery, Cerebral Palsy Association. All of these organizations are now likely in the next year or so to realize the impact of what we are debating here today, that two-page legislation. These organizations in Prince George are going to find out in the next year or two what it means to them.
When Ronald Reagan was in office, this government talked about the benefits trickling down. We know that does not happen. We know that under the Conservatives and under the Socreds and under the Liberals it is not the benefits trickling down, it is the benefits drying up. That usually is what happens under these governments.
The key aspect of all of this is that it is a way for this federal government and our provinces to work together to develop the kind of programming which means that

December 9, 1991
Government Orders
for the most unfortunate among us we have some assurances that they are going to be taken care of. There cannot be anything more important for a government to do. Raising and spending tax dollars is not more important than ensuring that its citizens are protected, fed and housed.
It is these kinds of programs that help do that. It is this kind of legislation that is starting to destroy those measures. We hope that some of the members opposite will go back to their ridings and find out what the impact of this legislation is going to be and what changes it is going to impact on them. I hope that when we vote on this bill they will reconsider the government's position, they will reconsider what the government is trying to do and join with members on this side of the House to oppose Bill C-32.1 hope they will do that in good spirit, in the spirit of friendship and in the spirit of the festive season.

Mr. Speaker, this is not the kind of bill that should get a very easy ride in this Chamber. What the bill and this government are doing, and the bill's predecessor Bill C-69 has done the same thing for the fiscal years 1990-91 and 1991-92, to those categories of people is so devastating and so unfair that this bill should get the roughest possible ride almost of any piece of legislation that comes before us here.
This is not something about which we can sit on hands and plead party loyalty, or whatever the glue is that keeps that crowd together over there. It is certainly not common sense. Common sense must have deserted that crowd long ago or it would have many months before coming unstuck as a team over the goods and services tax, just as an example. Eighty-five per cent of the people out there are against it and this crowd is refusing to turn up its hearing aid or is refusing to hear.
Nobody is so deaf as he who will not hear. Has the government not learned any lesson at all as a result of that shemozzle called the goods and services tax? Has it learned nothing as a result of the misery it has inflicted on people with its free trade agreement? How many times do you want to be hit over the head with baseball bats before you get simple messages? Are they all kamikazes over there, all suicide oriented in political terms? What is wrong with this crowd?
They look like normal people. They have nice shirts and ties, or dresses and so on as the case may be, but they behave most abnormally. They do not respond.
One time during my university days, I had the occasion to visit B. F. Skinner in his classroom at Harvard University. He showed me the famous Skinner box. He was the authority on the matter of the Pavlovian response, the stimulus and response connection.
This crowd, including my good friend from the riding of Red Deer, does not respond to the kind of stimulus that Dr. Skinner was talking about. As politicians or as human beings these people do not seem to be reached by things like human suffering. They seem to have awfully thick hides on matters that normal people respond to.
Go out there now to the shopping malls during Christmas and you see normal people who cannot walk past the Salvation Army or one of those Christmas kettles because it is an opportunity for them at this season to say in tangible terms that they feel for those who are down and out. They would like to do something tangible about it.
Compare that and trust that to these people over here. They do not seem to understand that the public, the poor, are going to be devastated one more time by this bill. The poor do not need another kick in the shin from this crowd. They need a bit of compassion. Times are rough out there. They are very rough. They are rough in my province of Newfoundland and Labrador, but they are rough in Ontario.
That is only half because of the NDP government. They would have been fairly rough anyway. They would have been rougher but that is another story. They are rough in Ontario.
Trying to spend the Liberal deficit.

I knew that would get a rise from my friend from British Columbia.
Great British Columbia. There are poor in British Columbia, too. There are poor all over this country.
That is right and you can blame it all on the new government after a couple of weeks in office?
My friend from Spadina should know a couple of things. One is that the government in Queen's Park has been there considerably longer than two weeks.
Trying to catch up on the Liberal deficit that the Liberals lied about.
He is not only being unparliamentary, he is also being inaccurate.
They concealed it.

He is also doing something else. He is giving one of the finest speeches he has given in this Chamber. I am going to make a deal with him.

I am thinking particularly about Vancouver East in British Columbia, and workers who have worked in the forest industry, members of the IWA who have been union members and have contributed so much to building the economy of British Columbia in the past. We have young people out on the streets getting into drugs and prostitution and who will never get out of that cycle. They would not be there if their families and communities were able to provide alternatives. In many cases the alternative means programs and support of social assistance during hard times.
It is absolutely essential that the federal share of the Canada Assistance Plan should be maintained in all provinces across Canada. We should have a 50/50 sharing of costs. Why should this government discriminate against three provinces, the so-called richest provinces which in reality have been the hardest hit by free trade and by the recession?
It is not only the impact on people and on services and on the cost of government which is so devastating, but it is really a promise and a responsibility of Confederation which is being broken by this government, particularly by this very regressive piece of legislation which erodes the Canada Assistance Plan, one of our most important social programs on the federal level.
I remember that when the Canada Assistance Plan was brought in, it was one of the better social programs established in Canada. When I was in social work and studying social policy, we always said how important it was. This was a progressive program which should be maintained along with our universal floor of social benefits as part of Canada's responsibility to its citizens.
We opposed very strongly moves in the 1970s and 1980s to try to change the 50/50 method of funding when some people, governments in particular, were trying to go for block funding or to open-ended funding such as

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in favour of the amendment that is before us today, which essentially does away with the single section of this act.
Basically this act is an attempt to starve the Canada Assistance Plan out of existence, starting with the three provinces that in a previous time were the wealthiest provinces in Canada. As a result of the policies of the current government, virtually every province in this country is operating on the edge of bankruptcy. It does affect first and foremost the three provinces British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario, which used to be considered under a more favourable political and economic system the have provinces of Canada. Under the current government they have been reduced like virtually every other province in the country to have not status.
My concern about this bill is that it does not even do what the government claims it is going to do. The government says this bill is necessary in order to cut the costs of government so that government can trim its expenses and reduce the deficit, which is largely a result of the interest and principle payments on the national debt. Statistics Canada has already pointed out that the major cause of the debt and therefore the major cause of the deficit in this country is not the social programs. It is

not program spending, as the Conservative government would have us believe.
Statistics Canada pointed out, in a study initially suppressed by the government until it was forced to release it, that 44 per cent of our national debt is due to tax and other concessions granted to large corporations, the wealthy and the powerful in this country.
Fifty per cent of that debt is attributable to the high interest rate policies, not only of this government but also of the former Liberal government. High interest rate policies have resulted in the ballooning of the debt. We now see a debt that is approaching something in the neighbourhood of $400 billion as a result of those tax concessions granted to the rich by both the Liberal and Conservative governments, as a result of the high interest rate policies.

The government should be targeting the 44 per cent by reducing some of those tax concessions to corporations, especially the ones not serving any useful purpose, that do not result in what the Conservatives believe in terms of the trickle down theory, because it does not trickle down. Everybody knows the reason it makes tax concessions to the wealthy and to corporations is so they can keep their wealth. They can keep their assets and not pass them down to other people. If you want something to trickle down, why serve the middle man? Why not pay that money directly to the people who require it and stand to benefit from it, the poor and those in need of social programs in this country.
It simply does not trickle down. It is a policy that does not work. It has been demonstrated decade after decade after decade that it does not work. Because it is a part of the ingrained ideology of Conservatives, and Liberals when they are in office, this theory continues to dominate the legislation in this country.
If we want to cut the deficit, do not do it by cutting social programs that everybody knows are not responsible for the deficit. Do it by cutting useless tax concessions to the rich. It has been pointed out in previous debates in this Parliament that we allow a billion dollars
in tax to go uncollected in order to finance business entertainment expenses for people involved in large corporations, wealthy people.
One billion dollars. We could reduce the deficit in a single year by one thirtieth if we cut business expense deductions. It does not do Canadians any good. There is no demonstrated value that comes from that business expense deduction. One billion dollars.
Eliminate the ability to deduct losses sustained in businesses overseas from profits earned in Canada. Again, that would save hundreds of millions of dollars from deductions which are allowed to Canadian businesses operating overseas, which serve no useful purpose for people in Canada. Billions, hundreds of millions. There are tax concessions that have been made to business by Liberal and Conservative governments over the years which serve no useful purpose and are responsible for 44 per cent of the national debt. Yet this government has done absolutely nothing to cut those. In fact over the last eight years, it has increased them. The rich are doing even better than they were in the past while the poor have been suffering more.
On October 14 I read an article in Maclean's which talks about one of the world's wealthiest men. The eighth wealthiest man in the world is Kenneth Thomson. According to Maclean's he makes over $27,800 an hour whether he is awake or asleep, living or dead; $27,800 an hour. There are many people in my constituency who would enjoy making in a year what that man makes in a single hour without lifting his hand or doing anything. He makes $4.4 million in a single week. This is the kind of person who benefits from the tax concessions that are granted by this government and by previous Liberal governments in order to assist him to make $27,800 an hour whether he is awake or asleep, no matter what he does. Nobody in Canada should be making that much without paying their fair share of the tax burden in this country.
We should not be cutting programs like the Canada Assistance Plan that basically benefits the poor, the sick and the people in need of government services until we start taking the fair share of taxes out of the $27,800 an hour that Ken Thomson is making by the sweat of other people's bodies.

I was reading in another magazine article that Canadian corporate executives are paid at least 100 times what production line workers are being paid. That is the spread between income of production line workers and Canadian corporate executives.
In Japan, a corporate executive makes only 16 times what a production line worker makes. Why are our corporate executives paid so much and why are they not paying their fair share of taxes? Instead, this government brings in legislation like this and who does it hit hardest? Abused and neglected children in need of protection, mentally and physically disabled persons, single parent families, seniors, the unemployed and the working poor, battered women, families and individuals in crisis.
What kind of a country are we living in when some people pay virtually no tax at all and are making $4.4 million a week, $27,800 an hour. The government does not touch them at all, except to augment their income with tax concessions, and yet legislation like this attacks the poorest of the poor, the people who need those services the most.
I would urge members, if they have any compassion at all, to read this legislation, understand what its impact is going to be and vote against it. Support this amendment by the New Democratic Party.

Legislation that was put through this place last week at report stage, I believe it was Bill C-20, sought to transfer this government's economic mismanagement on to the backs of the poorest provinces. This bill today seeks to transfer this government's economic mismanagement, not just on to the backs of the poorest provinces, but on to the backs of some of the poorest people in our country.
There is something inherently wrong with a society, a government, a country as wealthy as Canada, perhaps the wealthiest country in the world, when the government has squandered the resources and has been misdirected in where those resources should go. In the middle of the recession we are in-a lot worse than anything we have seen I think since the dirty thirties-in the wealthiest country in the world, we have in every community in

Canada line-ups at food banks. We have churches whose resources are stretched to their limits.
My riding of Dartmouth is a wealthy city. It is fairly well off with one of the lowest unemployment rates in Atlantic Canada and a large industrial base. But many times they forget that right in their midst, in the city of Dartmouth, there are individuals who because they cannot find a job or can only get a job that pays $5 an hour, cannot even afford to feed their children. They cannot afford to put decent clothes on the backs of their children. They are living in accommodations that no Canadian would be proud to say was a result of this great nation Canada and our absolute failure to redistribute wealth in this country.
I mentioned the churches in my riding of Dartmouth. I was absolutely stunned, shocked. I talked to Rev. Chang, an individual who has done much to try to reach out and help people in our community who have been shut out of the greatness of our economy, even during good times. He tells me that the number of individuals who have had to cash in their pride and integrity and stand in line waiting for a Christian handout from the churches in my community is growing almost exponentially. The people who have tried their very hardest to contribute, keep their integrity and provide for their offspring, have seen this recession bang the hell out of them.
At the same time that the ranks of the poor are multiplying like rabbits, we saw the spectacle last week of the Canadian chartered banks posting record profits. We talked about how wealthy this country is and how unfortunate it is that there are so many Canadians who cannot take advantage of the wealth and the resources that we have. That makes sure the wealth we have in this country belongs collectively to all of us. is what you are doing here. The province of Ontario is in the middle of a recession. When I think of the concept of an individual having to worry in this society today about whether or not their children are going to have a warm meal in their belly, it makes me sick.

I will tell anybody in this House or anybody out there on the far right wing of society that if they think that individuals in society choose to be poor, then they are crazy. It is demeaning, it destroys integrity, it destroys your ability to dream. Consider a child who is brought up in poverty- The biggest crime that we perpetrate on that child as a society is that we destroy their ability to dream. The New Democratic Party opposite has come in with a motion that basically says-and that is what we are debating here today-that the cap on CAP legislation or the enabling legislation would basically die because it is a one clause bill and they want to delete it with an amendment. deleted. But I also agree with those tens or hundreds of thousands of Canadians who say that we have to re-establish what our priorities are. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in favour of the motion that we have put forth with respect to capping the CAP. It is with a lot of regret and some emotion that I rise to speak to this bill because this is a bill that is indicative of what we are doing in this country to the poor and to those who are living below the poverty line and those who are struggling to keep above the poverty line.
We have in this country a major problem with the redistribution of wealth. Speaker after speaker in this party has been rising condemning that action and calling for some logic and some direction with respect to those Canadians who are deeply in need of an opportunity to get themselves out of the financial situation they are in.
The government has not been doing the job. There have been over the years a number of non-governmental organizations or NGOs that have been established. These groups are struggling as well. Although this particular motion and this particular bill only affects the three provinces Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia there are ripples right through the entire system. This is not the only bill that this government is putting forward. It is not the only action it has done. NGOs across this country are suffering and these are the ones who more and more are striving to fill the gap that is being left by governments.
In my own riding one of the most active groups is Transition House. Transition House is in Moose Jaw which is a small town compared to some of the cities in this country. It has a population of about 35,000. Transition House has one home. It is overcrowded. It is in need of expansion. They have no money for that. They used to be paid quarterly. They are now being paid monthly, making it very difficult for them to operate and to budget. Their funding has gone up far less than inflation has. In some years it has not gone up at all.
They are struggling. For example they were told by the former provincial government that they could manage

on one eight-hour shift. Transition House is open 24 hours a day. It has to be open 24 hours a day because no one knows when tragedy is going to occur or when a situation arises where a mother, a wife, is going to need Transition House. It is because they are being denied an opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, ever since I came into this House and even before that I have listened to some of the parliamentary debates. I keep hearing references, particularly from the government side, that this is the wealthiest nation in the world.
I guess if you were a member opposite circulating among the elite of society as you are wont to do, you probably would be saying that this is the wealthiest nation in the world. It would not really matter if it was not because you would be living well enough that if it was not the wealthiest one in the world, you would not be able to tell the difference anyway. There would be enough to buy the caviar, enough to buy the best wines, enough to take the best vacations, enough to hob-nob with the best people, enough money to have a private box in the SkyDome and enough money to be able to buy the prime shares on whatever stock exchange you felt like investing in: Toronto, Tokyo, Paris or London. I suspect you would invest in any and all of them because you would be putting your money where it did you the most good.
I suppose there are some people in this House of Commons who would say that we live in the wealthiest country in the world. I cannot say that. From my experience I know that we are not the wealthiest country in the world.

Wealthy is relative.

They have accomplished I am sure what is far beyond the dreams of Milton Friedman, far beyond the dreams of the monitors, far beyond the political philosophy of this Conservative government to enhance the pocketbooks of the rich in this country at the expense of the rest of the people.

I would suggest that the upper 20 per cent of this country are enormously well off. The upper 10 per cent are living in a wealthy situation that is impossible for the other 90 per cent of Canadians to even imagine.
In that instance, the Prime Minister was telling the truth. I must say that this country is unrecognizable. I must choose my words a little more judiciously. Since this government was elected in 1984, inflation has gone up by 29 per cent. Corporate taxes have gone up by 17 per cent albeit from 1986 to 1989 they actually declined in relation to the figure I am about to give you.
Corporate taxes since 1984 have gone up by 17 per cent. This is far less than inflation. I am not going to keep anyone in suspense because the individual taxes have gone up by 103 per cent. Is it any wonder that Canadians are becoming more and more impoverished every day? It is no mystery to me or to the people I talk to on the doorsteps of my constituency why they are so much worse off.
One of the main themes which I hear constantly on the doorstep of Saskatoon-Dundum is: "Ron, we have never been worse off. We have never been worse off". The figures show this.
In the 1960s, disposable income grew by 34 per cent. In the 1970s, disposable income grew by 22 per cent. This was still not too bad. Any of us who lived through the 1960s and the 1970s would realize that we did not do too badly. Things did improve. We were able to get a new car every three years or whatever it was. We were able to supply, without too much effort, the food, shelter and the education of our children.
In the 1980s disposable income grew by .5 per cent, one forty-fourth per cent of what it was in the seventies.
There is no mystery to the people I have talked to on the door steps. It is no mystery to me why some young people who started work in 1980 have not been able to make any progress at all in so far as being able to better themselves within our society.
Whatever happened to the concept of upward mobility? With figures like that, this who concept, this whole basis on which our society is economically established, upward mobility has come to a grinding halt. The predictions for 1992 and beyond are not that disposable income will grow, but that disposable income will decline.

Government Orders
We come to a bill like Bill C-32, a cap on CAP. The government says: "We have to do this. We have to cut back on these transfers to the provinces". It has got nothing to do with the debt. What it has to do with is the mean spirit of this government which takes a look at this block of people, mostly children, the elderly, the handicapped, single parent mothers, women who absolutely need the kind of help that this gives insofar as transition houses are concerned, houses for battered women. The government looks at this block of people in our society and says: "Those lazy, no good bums. People on welfare are lazy. If they are not going to work, we have to do something to try to force them to work".
It is completely beyond my comprehension how the government can give so many tax breaks. Someone else has pointed out that tax breaks to corporations account for 44 per cent of the federal debt. Fifty per cent of the federal debt is accountable for the high interest rates we have had to pay on the money that we had to borrow because getting it from the corporations was forgone.
The only reason these people are making these kinds of changes to the legislation, the only reason that they are holding this back, is because they believe that if they do this they will be able to somehow or another save the national debt. It escapes me how they can give the gigantic tax breaks to corporations and say that is an incentive. If they want to give an incentive to people who are poor, why can we not treat them the same as we do the corporations?
What is wrong with putting a decent amount of money into the pockets of the people who are receiving social assistance? It seems to me that an incentive for one ought to be an incentive for the other and this government in its mean spirit says: "No way".

Mr. Speaker, I am not necessarily happy to be taking part in this debate. It is not the kind of debate that Parliament should be having, given the circumstances the country is in.
I want to start by saying that the test of how civilized any society is is how well it treats its old, its sick, its poor and its children; how well it protects and preserves its environment, its wilderness and wildlife; how well it treats our aboriginal peoples; how well we help those
unfortunate human beings in the poor countries of the world.
Governments and societies that do not learn from history are condemned to repeat it and we are doing that now. The situation Canada is in now is equivalent to, and in some cases worse than, conditions we had in the dirty thirties. From 1930 to 1935 Tory governments under R. B. Bennett reigned.
I remember as a child of 10 hearing the grown-ups say: "Tory times are tough times". From 1935 to 1940 under the Liberals of Mackenzie King the tough times continued and in some respects got worse.
Both governments pleaded: "Where are you going to get the money?" The government is talking the same way now. It has not learned anything from recent history.
By 1940 every municipality, school board, provincial and federal government in this country were in debt and some were broke. My own province of Saskatchewan was bankrupt. You could not give its bonds away. There was no credit rating and the people were in the depths of despair and poverty.
"Where will we get the money", the government asks. There are several ways it can get the money. It can pick up another $1 billion or $2 billion by closing dozens of tax loopholes that still exist and benefit corporations and the wealthy. It could get the money by enforcing and going after the collection of what is politely called a tax gap, the collection of over $10 billion worth of unpaid taxes in this country. It was $10 billion in 1987. You can bet that it is a lot higher than that in 1991. In 1987 are the last figures that The Financial Post, and not some socialist periodical, came up with out of a report of Revenue Canada itself.
It talked about the tax evaders and the tax avoiders, the tax delinquents, all of those who can afford chartered accountants and lawyers to take advantage in every possible way of the tax law. Even when the tax avoider or tax evader loses to a successful challenge by Revenue Canada, there are a few types of taxpayers likely to change from non-compliers to compliers, to quote The Financial Post.

There is much to be done in this country and we have no excuse for not doing it. I have mentioned two areas in which billions are there to be obtained over the next year or so. I cannot say that I am speaking on behalf of my party in this instance. I am one of those who has been a close follower of John Maynard Keynes. In tough times you borrow and you spend and in good times you tax and repay.
If I had my way, over the next two years we would run the deficit up by another $2 billion, $3 billion or $4 billion, whatever is required. There would be short-term funding for food banks. My God, when I was a youngster in the dirty thirties they were called soup kitchens. It is refined now to food banks.
The fact is that it is a blot on our country and a disgrace for any government in any society to keep on putting up with that. The only way to get rid of deficits and debts is following policies of full employment. Why not establish a municipal fund from which municipalities can borrow? If the government can get the money at 7 per cent, then let the municipalities have it at 5 per cent and subsidize the interest rates or let them have it at 4 per cent, or in the first year pay all the interest charges.
The federal government is the one that has the complete control and authority on monetary and fiscal policy of this country, not any one province, not any municipality or school board and my hon. friend opposite cannot run away from it.
This country has scores of municipalities whose infrastructures need rebuilding and enlarging.
My God, we are still running raw sewage from Montreal into the St. Lawrence River. When are we going to see to it and do our part in helping to correct that?
Scores of municipalities across Canada have to fix and rebuild and modernize sewer and water systems, streets and sidewalks, power lines. That means jobs. It puts hundreds of thousands of people to work and they pay taxes. There is not a city or a large town in this country that does not have a list as long as your arm of people waiting for a house, waiting for a chronic care bed. Why are we not investing? A gain in construction means more and more jobs in low income and co-operative housing, federally, provincially and municipally.
Government Orders
We could put, over the next several years, a quarter of million people to work just cleaning up our air and our water. This will take some courage. It will take flying in the face of conventional wisdom and the typical Tory and Liberal line: "Where are you going to get the money?"
When we had a declaration of war all of a sudden there was a lot of money, lots and lots of money. I submit that we should now have a declaration of peace and make the same kinds of effort in fighting a war on poverty, illness, poor housing and our environment, to a greater extent than we ever did during the Second World War.
It is going to take that kind of effort, with the whole nation behind it. It has to be led by a federal government and it has to be led by this Parliament. The more we sit and wring our hands, the more we sit and rely on old ideological, worn out, wasted excuses and reasons. Where are we going to get the money? The money is there. What we need to do is challenge Canadians to roll up their sleeves and do all these things that need to be done. A policy of full employment will do more to wipe out deficits and substantially reduce if not eliminate the national debt.
That is what is required. We did it following the Second World War. If we translate our debt in 1945 into 1991 dollars, our debt then was as great or greater than it is now. It took us 10 or 12 years to pay it off. We financed the entire Second World War without a nickel of foreign investment, without a nickel.
We continue to sell out our economy for the sake of attracting foreign investors so that they can come in, make a profit and take the money out. They usually borrow the money from us. They financed the takeover of our economy and our country with our own money.
There are all those things to be done by this Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, actually it is not a pleasure to speak on this particular piece of legislation, but certainly we have to speak out against this and hope to bring the government to its senses on what it is doing to medicare.
I have just returned from Kamloops after having spent the last three days visiting people in their homes and talking to people in the shopping malls and going door to door throughout the small business community. When I

Government Orders
asked people if they are aware that the Mulroney government is in the process of eliminating medicare in Canada, they said: "No".
I reminded them of Bill C-69. They do remember that because it put a cap on the contribution the federal government provided for medical care and hospital care across Canada. They said they remembered that and they remembered people saying that this was the beginning of the end of medicare in Canada. I reminded them of this Bill C-32 which extends that process.
It is interesting to look at the pages and pages of testimony before the committee. I have the testimony of a number of expert witnesses in the health care field, the professional people who operate our health care system and people who have professionally studied the health care system of Canada. Virtually every one of these people who appeared before the committee pleaded, begged and said to stop this bill because it was the end of medicare in Canada, one of the hallmarks of Canadian citizenship.
We all know that each year there are hundreds of thousands of people, nay millions of people who would love to come to Canada, become landed immigrants and eventually citizens of this great country. They know there are a number of benefits that accrue to Canadian citizenship and one of them is medicare. It does not matter where you live in this country, whether it is in Newfoundland, the territories, British Columbia or the prairies. You have universal health care. Today we find that the United States of America is holding up the old Canadian model and saying: "This is the model that we want to have in the United States".
This government, these cabinet ministers and these back-bench Tories are in the process of dismantling the medicare system that is the hallmark of Canadian citizenship. We say that is wrong.
The people of Canada recognize what the government is doing to the country and our health care system. The people of Canada, through our efforts as members of the opposition, will find out that every single one of these experts in health care has said this legislation is the death-knell of medicare in Canada. The Conservatives should be chastised for initiating this legislation. They should be tossed out of office. Canadians will put the
New Democrats into office and we will once again put medicare back on the sound, financial footing that it should be on so that no matter where you are in Canada you will have access to this great system.
I cannot believe that my friends across the way are doing this. What do they have against sick people?
We are not and you know it.
What do they have against people who are ailing?
They are not your friends.
What nonsense. What poppycock.

There is my friend, the minister who says all these experts are wrong; oh, yes, he is right or his colleagues are right, but all the experts are wrong. I say I will throw my lot in with people who professionally know what health care is all about. I will say to my hon. friend-

Where are you going to get the
money?

He yells out where am I going to get the money. I will tell the minister where we are going to get the money. There are 69,000 profitable corporations in this country that do not pay any income tax at all. That is where some of the money should be coming from.
In any other country of the world when you inherit vast amounts of money and invest vast amounts of money you have to pay some taxes, but not in Canada. If you are a wealthy family and you are receiving millions and millions of dollars bequeathed upon you by your family, do you have to pay income tax in Canada? No. That is because those wealthy families have their friends across the way. They are called Conservative cabinet ministers who give privileges to the wealthy in this country and they pay for it by dismantling medicare.
What nonsense.

We say it is absolutely wrong. It is unCanadian. Why should we be surprised by an unCanadian act by this government. Show me an area, whether it is in broadcasting, the economy or social policy, where this government has done a single thing to benefit the people of Canada other than a handful of wealthy people. We cannot find it. We can look under every report and
December 9, 1991

initiative that has come out of this cabinet and we will not find it.
People around the world are perplexed because they know in their own countries they do not have this type of service. You think of what is going on, for example, in what used to be Yugoslavia today. The Croatian people are suffering by the tens and hundreds of thousands at the hands of a Serbian led army. People are defending themselves, their homes, their properties and their families with hunting rifles against tanks, artillery, air force and navy bombardment. The Serbian led Yugoslavian army, as we speak, is destroying historic monuments designated by the United Nations as historic treasures of the earth. They include old hospitals, churches, historic towns, cities and areas being bombarded presumably to break the Croatian people psychologically. They look at us and wonder why on earth we would be dismantling something as wonderful as medicare when they are struggling simply to maintain their own homeland against these barbaric forces.
When you think about it, 500,000 Croatian refugees are trying to leave the country wherever possible or seek refuge with family, friends or neighbours. An incredible hardship is being placed upon innocent people in that part of the world, and yet our government refuses to recognize the country of Croatia.
A number of Conservative backbenchers have asked the Prime Minister, as have others, to recognize Croatia but the government has not done it. Has it asked the UN Security Council to send in peacekeepers? No, it has not.
When I listen to the backbenchers of the Conservatives calling upon their government to take action, and they are being ignored, why would I be surprised at the government ignoring all of the experts when it comes to health care? When it does not even listen to its own backbenchers on something as life and death as the situation in Croatia, why would it listen to any of the people who understand health care recommending against the passage of this particular bill?
It is simply part of the old process. It is the father knows best approach to government. The Prime Minister says: "I am big brother. I know what is best for you Canadians. I know you do not agree, you do not support us, you do not support me, but I know what is best".
That is what a dictator says. That is what a leader of a totalitarian government says. At this sad time this is what
Government Orders
our Prime Minister says. He knows best, the people of Canada do not know what is best, the experts do not know what is best, but our Prime Minister does.
It is a sad day when we think that. For years and years we have developed one of the world's finest health care systems. This government, starting a few years ago with Bill C-69, decided to end medicare in Canada. It decided to have maybe some health care for profit in some parts of Canada. Some of the wealthier provinces will be able to sustain the absolute destruction of medicare, but the poorer parts of Canada will not be able to maintain the level of health care.
In terms of national standards they will be gone because the federal government has given up its leverage when it fails to participate at reasonable levels in the funding of health care. It is a very sad day. It is a sad day for Canada, a sad day for Canadians, and a sad day particularly for all of those men and women who dedicated their lives to establish a decent health care system in this country. Regardless of whether you were wealthy or poor, an eastern or western Canadian, no matter who you were, you had access to universal health care. In the future that will not be the case and it will be the Prime Minister of Canada and his government that will have used the wrecking ball on what we have known as medicare in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we know where the headaches are. They are right over there on the other side of the Chamber, right across from the opposition.
The government has brought in a bill to extend the cap on CAP for another three years. When the cap on CAP was first brought in, the godfather of the first cap on CAP was none other than the former Deputy Prime Minister, Erik Nielsen, old velcro lips. He was appointed chief honcho to take a look at all the government programs and see where he could cut fat and save money for the taxpayers.
He looked at the Canada Assistance Plan. He said: "It is a very good plan, a very good plan. It does a lot of good things". He then said: "You cannot have these open-ended agreements". The godfather of the cap on CAP is old velcro lips Erik Nielsen himself. When it comes to poor people, when it is time to transfer money to the less

December 9, 1991
Government Orders
fortunate people, he is a tightwad, a Scrooge. He is not the scrooge when it comes to his own spending.
Tell us about it.

The members says: "Tell us about it". Here is this guy who wants to spend like Santa and save like Scrooge. He spends like Santa on himself. This same Erik Nielsen recently put himself up in a Vancouver hotel for two nights at a cost of $1,000. He took a motor trip from Ottawa to Whitehorse, Yukon for $5,865. He took a slow car from Ottawa to Whitehorse, Yukon.
Did he buy the car?

That is a good question. Actually you could buy a new car with that money. He could buy one of the airlines in this country right now for that kind of money. Between November 1 and November 3 he was in Edmonton where he stayed at the Fantasyland Hotel for two nights at a cost of $403.20.
He has been in Fantasyland for years.

The entire trip from November 1 to November 3 cost taxpayers $1,888. Then he was off to Vancouver again from November 10 to November 12. The air fare was $1,805 and the hotel accommodation for two nights was $973.44. That is over $2,700 for a two-day visit.
This is the godfather of the cap on CAP. This is the person who sat and examined government accounts. It was this gentleman, Erik Nielsen, who said: "We have to tighten the belt and trim the fat".
We must remember he was in Fantasyland. This person is spending taxpayers' money. Why did he not think of cutting his own fat and saving taxpayers some money? I see government members on the other side. It is all right to applaud after the horse has left the bam, after the money has been spent.
It took an exhaustive search and fight through the freedom of information office to get information on this kind of spending. It seems it is an old adage: if you look after the pennies, the dollars will take care of themselves. Members on the other side represent only one interest: the fat cat interest. They are not interested in
the people who are suffering as a result of some of the things they have done.
That is part of the Tory culture. They have never been sensitive to the needs of people who work hard for a living. They have only been interested in and only benefited those who invest. They said: "Oh, no, you are not being fair". Government members say to me: "You are not being fair". Let me try to be fair for the record.
I am looking at The Financial Post and at an article that appeared on August 29, 1990. It says: "Big corporations leading tax evaders". We are talking about tax evasion here, not tax avoidance. There is a big difference.
Here is what the article says: "Revenue Canada estimates that the so-called tax gap, the amount owed but not paid by Canadians, hit $10 billion in 1987, the last year for which an estimate was available". That is almost four times the 1977 level.
We are talking about tax not collected. When a widow in my riding owes a few hundred dollars to Revenue Canada, we can see how tough it is on her. It sends out the knee breakers, the letters. It threatens. It is tough. It is tough in collecting.
Then the member of Parliament gets involved and says to the Revenue Canada people: "How come you are so tough on poor people? Inco owes you all kinds of taxes. Why do you not get as tough with them? Why do you not go over there and tell them that you are going to break their knees, that you are going to send some boys over?" Why does the government not do that? Why does it not put a lien on the mine or garnishee its receipts?
It will not do that. It will not do that at all. I want to suggest very seriously that it deliberately complicates the tax laws of this country so that its corporate friends avoid paying the tax.
They should read the tax act. They all get up and piously say: "We have to simplify the language of the tax act". There is piety over on the other side about the simplicity of the tax laws. The government has been in office now for seven years and we have not seen any simplification of the tax laws of this country. The
December 9, 1991

government has made them more complex, more complicated. Corporate tax law is extremely complicated.
What does a corporation do? It simply goes out, hires fancy tax consultants, tax lawyers and tax accountants and it avoids paying the taxes. Even when it gets nailed, it does not pay it. It appeals it and it goes through a whole procedural rigmarole and it never, for years, pays any taxes. It does not for years.
I suppose some of them are skiddled off to the sunshine states where they can set up shop and avoid paying. The tax structure has been so jiggered that now the government collects about 45 per cent of its revenues from ordinary taxpayers. From its corporate friends, it collects about 9 per cent of the total revenues.
This is a new switch. This is a new concept of a medieval view of Robin Hood. Robin Hood used to take from the wealthy to give to the poor.
