Mr. Speaker, it is wonderful to be complimented by someone who gives bald men a bad name in the House of Commons.
The amendment before the House of Commons today is an amendment which deals with Bill C-32. Bill C-32 is the bill that will extend the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan up until 1995. It is an extension of Bill C-69 which became known in infamy throughout Canada over the last year when people realized that through this bill there was an attack, as my friend from Kamloops has
Government Orders
said, on the medical care system and the health system in Canada and on the post-secondary system. We spoke to that part of the extension last week.
Bill C-32 deals directly with the Canada Assistance Plan which deals with the transfer payments of the federal government through to the provinces for matters of social assistance and all those matters interprovincial-ly and within the provinces that deal with, for the most part, those who are less able to care for themselves through usually no fault of their own.
The amendment from my friend and colleague from Essex-Windsor is an amendment that would simply delete that extension. By taking away clause 1 of Bill C-32 it effectively does away with the bill and we go back to the system as it was set up and as it should be.
I speak in favour of that but in opposition to the idea behind Bill C-32.
In the Montreal Gazette on December 7,1991 a letter from Southam News' Eric Beauchesne points out in a headline: "Abandoning the job hunt". In that article he says:
Thousands of unemployed, frustrated by a lack of job opportunities, quit looking for work last month and that's all that kept unemployment from rising above an already dismal 10.3 per cent, analysts said yesterday.
Employment fell by 49,000 in November but the unemployment rate remained at October's level because 45,000 workers also dropped out of the labour force, Statistics Canada said.
Statistics Canada further reported the week of December 7 that job prospects are their bleakest in seven years.
What does the unemployment rate and those that dropped out of the job market have to do with the Canada Assistance Plan? Where do these people go? They can no longer get unemployment insurance because this government changed the rules. It made it harder for people to get unemployment insurance and for those who can get on the unemployment insurance rolls. It shortened the period they can continue getting benefits.
In today's job market, as has been shown in this article and many others, it is clear that these people want jobs. They want to work. They need money to keep food on the table for their families. The average family has over

December 9, 1991
Government Orders
two children each. It is these children who unfortunately suffer as a result of the poverty of their parents.
When they can no longer get unemployment insurance, they run through any savings that they have been fortunate enough to carry over the years. Where do they turn?
They turn to social assistance. The welfare programs are carried on by provinces or in some provinces by the larger cities themselves. They have to turn to these people.
Those 45,000 who dropped out of the market are some of those same people who are now looking at alternative methods of financing themselves, often and probably through social assistance. The money that comes from that social assistance has to be gained somewhere. By robbing Peter to pay Paul, the federal government is shirking responsibility to those people who have been hurt by the fiscal and monetary policies that this government has been following since 1984.
In the evidence given before the finance committee looking into Bill C-32, Lise Corbeil of the National Anti Poverty Organization, stated: "Bill C-32 will have an incredible negative impact on poor people. They are asked to tighten their belts in the name of deficit reduction, to trim the fat from their expenses while the National Council on Welfare study proved that there is absolutely no fat to trim when you live on welfare. To the federal government, CAP is one among many budget items on an expense sheet. It is just a line. To people living on social assistance, CAP is a lifeline. Welfare is their means of livelihood. It is not an intellectual exercise to try to balance a budget".
That brings out very graphically what the problem is with this government capping the Canada Assistance Plan.
As the unemployment roles increase and more people go on welfare and social assistance and as more people transfer into provinces such as Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta, the three provinces hurt by the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, the provinces are forced into either cutting back services or increasing taxes within those provinces that most need the assistance of the federal government because of that immigration from other areas of the country and other areas of the world. Those people come into these most desirable
areas such as Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia and it is these three provinces that have had their assistance capped by the Canadian government.
Who is hurt by this policy? The poor, the poverty stricken, those who have nowhere to go, those who depend on this as a lifeline. It is a lifeline of the children who are hurt through the lack of assistance from this government.
It is interesting to note that one child in six in Canada is classified as poor. More than 1 million children under the age of 18 live in poverty. It is an interesting and sad commentary on today's life in Canada that almost half of the Canadians who rely on food banks are children, an estimated 225,000 children.
Shameful.

It is shameful. It is unfortunate. It is something this government must take into consideration. It must look at its policies. Many poor children live in families struggling on 50 to 60 per cent of poverty line income.
At a time such as this, leading into Christmas, it has become more and more apparent: the long line-ups at food banks; the number of people living in poverty; those who will not be able to sit down to turkey and stuffing or have gifts under the tree; those who will not be able to enjoy Christmas as Christmas should be enjoyed, by children and by all of us. It is hard to remember the joy of the season when you do not have food on the plate to feed your children and as a child your stomach is empty.
We have to do something about this bill and I suggest to this House that the way to do it is by supporting the amendment. I would ask this House to consider that amendment strongly and pass it.

Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that the very parliamentary day following December 6, the National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence Against Women, that we should be standing in this House debating a bill that extends the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan.
On Friday members of the government were standing in this place decrying violence against women and saying that we must end the situation that creates violence against women. They were saying that we in this House

of Commons must take effective action to end violence against women. They were saying that we must provide the services that battered women so desperately need in this country to escape from violent situations.
It is ironic and it is sad. It is sad because this Bill C-32 will have a chilling effect on the building of shelters for battered women. The Canada Assistance Plan is the only funding mechanism in place right now for providing shelters for battered women. Now the government is extending this limit on funding until 1995. It is such hypocrisy. All the people in the House heard it say on Friday: "We must take action to end violence". Yet it is cutting from the very services that these women so desperately need to get out of violence and to break the cycle of violence.
It is beyond me. It is beyond me how this government can brag over and over again as it did again on Friday about its family violence initiative fund and then cut and then continue to cut from the services that women need.
It cut the social programs. It cut shelters for battered women with this bill. It is cutting child care spaces as well with this bill and we all know what a desperate need there is for child care in this country.
CAP is the only funding mechanism in place for child care spaces. The government knows how badly they are needed. The situation in Canada for child care is desperate. In fact today when a woman becomes pregnant in Canada, probably the first thing she does after getting that confirmation from her doctor, if she is a woman who works outside the home, is go and put her name on a list at a child care centre. She is hoping that by the time her child is two years old she may have child care. But they still wait years and years and years to find suitable child care in this country.
This government has refused to honour the promises it made in 1984, the promises it made in 1988 and the promises that it has made in throne speeches over and over again to provide Canadians with a national child care program. Now it is extending the funding cuts again from the only vehicle in this country that funds child care spaces.
It does this with the rationale of saying: "We are only capping the funds to five per cent". It calls it capping. In reality we know with the rate of inflation and everything
Government Orders
else it is an actual cut in services. It says it is doing this in the name of fiscal restraint and it says it is only doing it to the rich provinces that can afford to take this capping. This government also knows that over 50 per cent of the poor in this country live in these three provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
In my province of British Columbia we have a food bank in Vancouver that is there simply and only for women and children. What has it come to in this country when volunteer organizations and church organizations are organizing food banks for women and children? The fact is that 50 per cent of the poor live in those three provinces. They are just as poor as the poor in other parts of Canada.
Those women who are beaten in those provinces are just as black and blue, just as degraded as the women in any other part of Canada.
This bill is just another example of how this government has decided to place the burden of paying off the debt on the shoulders of those who can least afford it, those who are not responsible for the debt.
Statistics Canada has shown that the spending on social programs is only responsible for 6 per cent of the national debt. In reality it is the tax breaks to wealthy people and to corporations that are responsible for 44 per cent of the debt.
The government has not targeted the cause of the debt to resolve it. Corporate taxes from 1986 to 1989 declined by approximately 20 per cent even though those profits increased by 34 per cent during the same time.
In fact the Statistics Canada figures in April show that taxes increased the most from 1988 to 1989 for those on the second lowest rung of the income ladder, with an increase of 1.1 per cent. But those in the highest income levels saw taxes rise by .9 per cent and those in the second highest by only .3 per cent.
Is this what the government means by tax fairness? Is this its idea of what it calls tax reform? It seems more like tax deform than tax reform.
These figures only confirm that those who should be paying for the deficit are not. Ttx loopholes for the wealthy and for big corporations amount to more than $6 billion a year. For $6 billion we could have a heck of a

December 9, 1991

good child care program in this country, one that meets the needs of all of Canada's children.
The Tories have not made a single move to get rid of the loopholes that were caused by the previous Liberal government. It had its commissions when it was in government and ignored the recommendations it received for tax fairness, just like this government does.
The largest group of people affected by this bill, of course, are children; the children and the poor of this country. Contrast the government's action with its commitment to eliminate child poverty by the year 2000. I want to ask the government how removing money from social assistance will help children to escape from poverty. It is ironic that Canada plans to ratify the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, since Bill C-32 will have a devastating effect on the health and the well-being of the children in this country who rely on social assistance, over a million children in Canada.
We are one of the wealthiest nations in the world and we still have a million children living in poverty. We are second only to the U.S. in the level of child poverty in the industrialized world.
These children, these battered women and the poor of this country are the ones who are being asked to pay the price for the tax loopholes that are offered to the wealthy and to the big corporations. I want to ask, is that just? Is that fair? Is that tax reform? I do not think so.
As if Bill C-32 is not causing enough damage, when you put it together with all the other regressive actions of this government the future for Canada looks very bleak indeed. Bill C-21 will make UI harder to get. The de-indexation of family allowance benefits means that families get less and less and children get less and less each year. There is the clawback on family allowances and old age pensions.
Further cuts to social assistance, cuts to health and post-secondary education, Bill C-69 and Bill C-20 are threatening the future of medicare and accessible postsecondary education for all of Canada's people.
There is still no sign of a child care policy. Promise, promise, promise, nothing but broken promises from this government. This is just another Tory attack on social programs which the government claims it is doing in the
name of financial restraint. But it is clear this is a move about politics. This is politics, not money, not fiscal restraint, and these politics amount to more breaks for the friends of the government and a life of poverty and hunger for millions of Canadians who are burdened under the weight of high taxes and a tattered and weakened social safety net beneath them.
This really is a government of grinches at this time of the year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The present economic situation is disastrous, Mr. Speaker, and it is definitely a bad time to be capping the Canada Assistance Plan.
The poverty rate in the greater Montreal area is at an all-time high. More that 15 per cent of the people living on the island of Montreal is made up of poor families, that is to say 200,000 more than in the four Atlantic provinces combined. At least 60 per cent of welfare recipients in Montreal have been on the welfare rolls for two years. The unemployment rate in the Montreal area-the statistics were released on Friday-is still 12 per cent. What can be done to get out of this slump? During these difficult economic times, the government wants to cap the Canada Assistance Plan.
According to Statistics Canada, 45,000 workers have been dropped from the list of people looking for work not because they found jobs, but for the majority because their unemployment insurance benefits ran out and they are now on welfare.
My office is in the same building as the welfare office and I can assure you that every time I take the elevator I see unhappy people. There are a great many of them and in my riding as elsewhere the welfare office cannot keep up.
Our unemployment insurance offices cannot keep up with the demand. What about our welfare offices? There are over 10,000 homeless people in Montreal alone who spend the winter in subway stations. With the freezing temperatures we have in this country, what do you think they are going to live on this winter? Food banks-I just happened to be reading in the newspapers last weekend
December 9, 1991

that Sun Youth, an organization which does a great job, cannot keep up with the demand the Holiday Season being just around the corner. The shelves are empty. There is not enough food to go around.
It surely is not a good time to make cuts, to cap public assistance. Last Friday we heard from both sides of this House statements on violence against women as well as on violence in general. Every morning I look at the newspaper when I get up and every day I read that someone somewhere was shot or killed. Why? Because they have nowhere to stay, nothing to eat, no job, nothing. We can see the result: increasing violence. The number of violent crimes is increasing every day.
The government has the responsibility to do something, to help in this very difficult period. There will be, I hope, as you do, Mr. Speaker, better times in this country, but for the moment the situation is so bad that we have to help people in need so they too can have some hope.
In Montreal-and this is not the first time this is mentioned in the House-exams had to be scheduled so as to coincide with the receipt of welfare cheques, because after a couple of weeks there is no money left and children come to school hungry, a fact which is not exactly conducive to good performance during exams. This is so serious it is almost unbelievable.
In Montreal East-I am giving figures for the whole of the island of Montreal, but there is the west, the centre and the east-it is totally unacceptable. We have never seen such a situation before.
I urge the government to revise its plan, to drop its decision to cap welfare payments, and to give to those who are in real need. During the Christmas season it is important to give. It is important for people to believe there is light at the end of the tunnel, that there is hope for a better tomorrow. What if we abandon them? Of course the government will argue it is strapped for money, but is it the right time to make those cuts? Is it the right time to deal with those financial problems?
The government had a number of good years. There were years when the economy was in good shape, and that is when it should have dealt with those problems. Unfortunately they were incapable of dealing with those economic problems and that is why we are in this recession today. The government keeps cutting. If you
Government Orders
keep squeezing a lemon when there is no juice left, the result is the kind of violence we see every day not just in Montreal-I am from Montreal so I am very aware of this-but across Canada.
I hope the government will be able to listen to members on both sides of the House, because I am sure there are government members like yourself, Mr. Speaker, who share this view. Perhaps, in the spirit of Christmas, we should set aside political partisanship, withdraw this bill and increase welfare payments so that Canadians living in poverty can hope to have a Merry Christmas.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of this motion doing radical surgery on Bill C-32. It is an amendment but it is radical surgery.
This is a bill that imposes a significant amount of belt tightening on our public finances in this country. It is belt tightening but we must look and ask who we are asking to tighten their belts. Who is going to do the belt tightening here? It is the poor and the hungry. It is not those who have the decent pay cheque coming in every week and who still have a job in this recession. It is the poor and the hungry.
The government says this is just a marginal impact on transfer payments, the Canada Assistance Plan payments that are paid to the provinces. It is marginal and puts a limit on the increases but every single dollar of that margin is being borne on the backs of the poor and the hungry. It is not marginal for that class of people in this country.
What was a two-year plan is now a five-year plan. It is extended out another three years and involves another $2 billion. I want to ask the House to contrast the fight that was waged by the Public Service in this town and across the country on the matter of the zero, three and three wage control and the imposed arbitration. That was a big fight. That was a strike. There was dislocation of government services right across this country and yet this bill is going to impact just as much and maybe more on the poor and hungry of this country.
Where are they? I would venture to suggest that many of them do not even know what is happening here. Who is here to speak for the poor and the hungry right here

Government Orders
now as we approach the Christmas season? The timing is terrible.
The reason why the belt tightening has been made necessary is the failure of this government to address its fiscal management in the mid-1980s. It ran up a deficit that began in 1982 and 1983. It escalated and it kept on coming year after year right through the good years when we had an opportunity to put our finances in order.
I am very critical of the government for permitting this situation to occur.
